name: drawn_morph
description: >
  A drawn morph, heard: five boxes that draw two strokes on the document's drawing, read them back,
  pair their points with matchPoints, morph between them, and play the morph as pitch.

  Run `shapes` first: it draws a blue circle named "from" and a red heart named "to". `paired`
  reads both strokes back with notation.named, resamples each to 240 points evenly spaced by arc
  length (resampleByLength), matches them one-to-one (matchPoints) and draws the pairs, matched
  and by list index. `morph` draws five steps of each pairing. `spread` plots the size of the cloud
  through the morph. `play` turns the morph, out to the heart and back, into 32 notes whose pitch
  is that size, and renders two cycles of each pairing offline into audio players.
  To morph your own shapes, draw two closed pen strokes (Alt+D, then P) and follow the comment in
  `shapes`.

  Companion to public/docs/chain_drawn_morph.md. Pure CPU; no Window, no Renderer, no audio device.
operations:
  - create:
      box: dm_shapes
      name: shapes
      frame: { x: 20.0, y: 40.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Two strokes, drawn from code into the document's drawing: a circle named "from" and a
          // heart named "to". Running it again replaces them.
          notation { morphShapes() }
          // To morph two strokes you drew yourself (Alt+D, P), delete the line above and use:
          //   val mine = notation.strokes.filter { it.handDrawn }.takeLast(2)
          //   notation.edit(mine[0]) { name = "from" }
          //   notation.edit(mine[1]) { name = "to" }
          println(notation.strokes.map { "${it.label}: ${it.points.size} points" })
  - create:
      box: dm_paired
      name: paired
      frame: { x: 20.0, y: 520.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Read the strokes back, give each 240 evenly spaced points, and pair them.
          val from = notation.named("from")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
          val to = notation.named("to")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
          val match = matchPoints(from, to)
          val partner = match.reorder(to)
          val cx = from.sumOf { it.x.toDouble() } / from.size; val cy = from.sumOf { it.y.toDouble() } / from.size
          fun chord(a: Vec2, b: Vec2, dx: Double) = FLine().moveTo(a.x + dx, a.y).lineTo(b.x + dx, b.y).also {
              it.thickness = 0.8
              it.color = okhsl(atan2(a.y - cy, a.x - cx) * 180 / PI + 360, 0.85, 0.6, 0.9)
          }
          // Left: the matching. Right: point i of one stroke to point i of the other.
          lines(from.indices.map { chord(from[it], partner[it], -220.0) } + from.indices.map { chord(from[it], to[it], 220.0) },
              w = 760.0, h = 380.0, fitToSize = true)
          val byIndex = from.indices.sumOf { (from[it].x - to[it].x).toDouble().pow(2) + (from[it].y - to[it].y).toDouble().pow(2) }
          println("squared travel: matched %.0f, by list index %.0f".format(match.squaredCost, byIndex))
  - create:
      box: dm_morph
      name: morph
      frame: { x: 20.0, y: 1000.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Five steps of the morph: matched on top, by list index below.
          val from = notation.named("from")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
          val to = notation.named("to")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
          val partner = matchPoints(from, to).reorder(to)
          val cx = from.sumOf { it.x.toDouble() } / from.size; val cy = from.sumOf { it.y.toDouble() } / from.size
          fun dot(p: Vec2, dx: Double, dy: Double, colour: Vec4) = FLine().also { f ->
              val x = (p.x - cx) * 0.5 + dx; val y = (p.y - cy) * 0.5 + dy
              f.moveTo(x - 2, y - 2).lineTo(x + 2, y - 2).lineTo(x + 2, y + 2).lineTo(x - 2, y + 2).lineTo(x - 2, y - 2)
              f.color = colour; f.filled = true; f.stroked = false
          }
          val steps = listOf(0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0)
          lines(steps.indices.flatMap { s ->
              morphBetween(from, partner, steps[s]).map { dot(it, s * 200.0, 0.0, vec(0.1, 0.45, 0.85, 1.0)) } +
                  morphBetween(from, to, steps[s]).map { dot(it, s * 200.0, 200.0, vec(0.88, 0.2, 0.2, 1.0)) }
          }, w = 1000.0, h = 400.0, fitToSize = true)
  - create:
      box: dm_spread
      name: spread
      frame: { x: 20.0, y: 1480.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // How big the in-between cloud is (RMS distance from its centre), for both pairings.
          val from = notation.named("from")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
          val to = notation.named("to")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
          val partner = matchPoints(from, to).reorder(to)
          val ts = (0..50).map { it / 50.0 }
          showSignals(
              "matched" to ts.map { spreadOf(morphBetween(from, partner, it)) },
              "by list index" to ts.map { spreadOf(morphBetween(from, to, it)) },
              x = ts, title = "how big the cloud is, through the morph", xTitle = "t", yTitle = "spread", channel = "spread",
          )
  - create:
      box: dm_play
      name: play
      frame: { x: 20.0, y: 1960.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // The morph out to the heart and back as 32 notes: MIDI 72 at the circle's size, an
          // octave lower for every halving. Edit the loop to change what you hear.
          val from = notation.named("from")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
          val to = notation.named("to")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
          val voice = patVoice(wave = PatWave.TRIANGLE, decay = 0.004, sustain = 0.6)
          for ((label, partner) in listOf("matched" to matchPoints(from, to).reorder(to), "by list index" to to)) {
              val notes = mutableListOf<TimedNote>()
              val spread0 = spreadOf(from)
              for (k in 0 until 32) {
                  val t = if (k < 16) k / 15.0 else (31 - k) / 15.0   // out to the heart, then back
                  val midi = 72 + 12 * log2(spreadOf(morphBetween(from, partner, t)) / spread0)
                  notes += TimedNote(k * 0.25, k * 0.25 + 0.25, midi)
              }
              println("$label: lowest note %.2f".format(notes.minOf { it.note }))
              showPatAudio(patTimed(notes, beats = 8.0), cycles = 2, cps = 0.25, voice = voice, channel = label)
          }
  - execute:
      box: dm_shapes
      property: code
  - execute:
      box: dm_paired
      property: code
  - execute:
      box: dm_morph
      property: code
  - execute:
      box: dm_spread
      property: code
  - execute:
      box: dm_play
      property: code

before:
# A Drawn Morph, Heard

Two strokes on the drawing layer, a circle and a heart. `notation` reads them back as lists of
points, `resampleByLength` gives each the same number of points, evenly spaced, and `matchPoints`
pairs every point of the circle with a point of the heart. Moving each point toward its partner is
a morph. The size of the cloud as it moves is a number per step, and played as pitch it is a tune
you can hear the shape change in.

The two strokes on this page are drawn by code, but two strokes you draw by hand and name "from" and
"to" are read the same way.

## Two strokes, paired

`morphShapes()` draws the circle in blue, starting on its right and going round anticlockwise, and
the heart in red, starting at its bottom point and going clockwise. The circle is drawn the way a
hand draws one, slowly off the start and into the end, so its points are bunched there. The box
reads both strokes back by name, resamples them, and matches them:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/chain_drawn_morph/paired.png" wait="3" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1180" h="460" padding="18" timeout="90" name="chain-drawn-morph-paired" embed=true alt="Two copies of a circle and a heart joined by coloured chords. On the left each circle point is joined to the heart point matchPoints gave it, short chords that fan outward evenly; on the right each is joined to the heart point with the same list index, long chords that cross the whole figure. A table beside them gives the point counts and the total squared travel of each pairing."}
notation { morphShapes() }
val drawnFrom = notation.named("from")!!.points
val drawnTo = notation.named("to")!!.points
val from = drawnFrom.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
val to = drawnTo.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
val match = matchPoints(from, to)
val partner = match.reorder(to)

:::fold draw the pairs both ways, and the table
fun chord(a: Vec2, b: Vec2, dx: Double) = FLine().moveTo(a.x + dx, a.y).lineTo(b.x + dx, b.y).also {
    it.thickness = 0.8
    it.color = okhsl(atan2(a.y - 260.0, a.x - 520.0) * 180 / PI + 360, 0.85, 0.6, 0.9)
}
lines(from.indices.map { chord(from[it], partner[it], -220.0) } + from.indices.map { chord(from[it], to[it], 220.0) },
    w = 760.0, h = 380.0, fitToSize = true)
val byIndex = from.indices.sumOf { (from[it].x - to[it].x).toDouble().pow(2) + (from[it].y - to[it].y).toDouble().pow(2) }
markdown("travel", """
| | |
|---|---|
| points drawn, circle and heart | ${drawnFrom.size} and ${drawnTo.size} |
| points after resampling | ${from.size} and ${to.size} |
| squared travel, matched (left) | ${"%.0f".format(match.squaredCost)} |
| squared travel, by list index (right) | ${"%.0f".format(byIndex)} |
""", width = 420)
:::endfold
```

Matched, each chord is short and they fan out together. Paired by index, the circle's first point
goes to the heart's first point, which is on the other side of the figure, and every other pair is
dragged round with it. The readout is the total squared distance each pairing asks the points to
travel.

Resampling is what makes the two strokes comparable. Excalidraw keeps a stroke as the points the
pen produced, so the two strokes have different numbers of points, and the circle's are crowded at
its start. `resampleByLength(n)` walks the stroke by arc length and places exactly `n` points along
it at equal distances; `closed = true` treats the stroke as a loop, so the last point is not a
repeat of the first.

## The morph

`morphBetween(from, partner, t)` puts each point a fraction `t` of the way to its partner. Five
steps of each pairing, top matched and bottom by index:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/chain_drawn_morph/morph.png" wait="3" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1180" h="460" padding="18" timeout="90" name="chain-drawn-morph-morph" embed=true alt="Two rows of five dot clouds going from a circle to a heart. In the top row, the matched one, every in-between step is a shape between the two, with a few dozen points leaving the outline for the heart's top cleft. In the bottom row, paired by list index, the middle steps fold in on themselves and shrink toward the centre before opening out into the heart."}
notation { morphShapes() }
val from = notation.named("from")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
val to = notation.named("to")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
val partner = matchPoints(from, to).reorder(to)

:::fold draw five steps of each
fun dot(p: Vec2, dx: Double, dy: Double, colour: Vec4) = FLine().also { f ->
    val x = (p.x - 520.0) * 0.5 + dx; val y = (p.y - 260.0) * 0.5 + dy
    f.moveTo(x - 2, y - 2).lineTo(x + 2, y - 2).lineTo(x + 2, y + 2).lineTo(x - 2, y + 2).lineTo(x - 2, y - 2)
    f.color = colour; f.filled = true; f.stroked = false
}
val steps = [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]
lines(steps.indices.flatMap { s ->
    morphBetween(from, partner, steps[s]).map { dot(it, s * 200.0, 0.0, vec(0.1, 0.45, 0.85, 1.0)) } +
        morphBetween(from, to, steps[s]).map { dot(it, s * 200.0, 200.0, vec(0.88, 0.2, 0.2, 1.0)) }
}, w = 1000.0, h = 400.0, fitToSize = true)
:::endfold
```

Paired by index, the points cross the middle of the figure to reach their partners, so halfway
through the cloud is folded in on itself and smaller than either shape. Matched, the outline stays
an outline, except for the few points that the first figure shows as long chords on its left: the
matching sends them from the top of the circle down into the cleft between the heart's two lobes,
and they cross the inside of the shape to get there.

## The morph, as a number and as sound

`spreadOf(points)` is how big a cloud is: the root-mean-square distance of its points from their
centre. Follow it from `t = 0` to `t = 1` for both pairings:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/chain_drawn_morph/spread.png" wait="3" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1180" h="300" padding="18" timeout="90" name="chain-drawn-morph-spread" embed=true alt="Two curves of cloud size against morph fraction. The matched curve falls in a straight line from the circle's size to the heart's; the index-order curve falls far below both before rising to the heart's size at the end."}
notation { morphShapes() }
val from = notation.named("from")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
val to = notation.named("to")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
val partner = matchPoints(from, to).reorder(to)
notation.clear()   // read: take the strokes down so they do not lie over the plot
val ts = (0..50).map { it / 50.0 }
showSignals(
    "matched" to ts.map { spreadOf(morphBetween(from, partner, it)) },
    "by list index" to ts.map { spreadOf(morphBetween(from, to, it)) },
    x = ts, title = "how big the cloud is, through the morph", xTitle = "t", yTitle = "spread", channel = "spread",
)
```

To hear it, the morph goes out to the heart and back in 32 steps, a quarter of a beat each. Each
step is a note: MIDI 72 when the cloud is the circle's size, an octave lower for every halving of
it. `patTimed` makes the notes a pattern of eight beats, and `patRenderStereo` plays it through
`patVoice`, a simple triangle-wave synth voice:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val notes = mutableListOf<TimedNote>()
val spread0 = spreadOf(from)
for (k in 0 until 32) {
    val t = if (k < 16) k / 15.0 else (31 - k) / 15.0   // out to the heart, then back
    val midi = 72 + 12 * log2(spreadOf(morphBetween(from, partner, t)) / spread0)
    notes += TimedNote(k * 0.25, k * 0.25 + 0.25, midi)
}
val audio = patRenderStereo(patTimed(notes, beats = 8.0), cycles = 2, cps = 0.25,
    voice = patVoice(wave = PatWave.TRIANGLE, decay = 0.004, sustain = 0.6))
```

The matched morph, twice through:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin audio="assets/chain_drawn_morph/drawn-morph-matched.wav" audio-spec="drawn-morph-matched" audio-renderer="afield.audio.synth.DrawnMorphDocs" embed=true hidden=true name="chain-drawn-morph-matched-audio"}
// Offline-rendered by DrawnMorphDocs.renderWav("drawn-morph-matched").
```

The same loop with `to` in place of `partner`, the points paired by index:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin audio="assets/chain_drawn_morph/drawn-morph-index.wav" audio-spec="drawn-morph-index" audio-renderer="afield.audio.synth.DrawnMorphDocs" embed=true hidden=true name="chain-drawn-morph-index-audio"}
// Offline-rendered by DrawnMorphDocs.renderWav("drawn-morph-index").
```

The heart is smaller than the circle, so the first falls steadily to the heart's pitch and climbs
back. The second falls about twice as far and climbs back before it reaches the heart, which is the
fold in the bottom row of the morph above.

The pitch the box computes, step by step, for both:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/chain_drawn_morph/pitch.png" wait="3" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1180" h="300" padding="18" timeout="90" name="chain-drawn-morph-pitch" embed=true alt="Two staircases of MIDI pitch over 32 steps, out and back. The matched one descends in a straight line to the heart's pitch and back; the index-order one drops about twice as far at the middle of each half. Below, the lowest note of each."}
notation { morphShapes() }
val from = notation.named("from")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
val to = notation.named("to")!!.points.resampleByLength(240, closed = true)
val matched = DrawnMorphDocs.morphNotes(from, matchPoints(from, to).reorder(to))   // the loop above
val byIndex = DrawnMorphDocs.morphNotes(from, to)
notation.clear()

showSignals("matched" to matched.map { it.note }, "by list index" to byIndex.map { it.note },
    title = "pitch per step", xTitle = "step", yTitle = "MIDI", channel = "pitch")
markdown("dips", "lowest note, matched: %.2f  \nlowest note, by list index: %.2f".format(matched.minOf { it.note }, byIndex.minOf { it.note }), width = 400)
```

## Drawing your own

Open [drawn_morph](agent_transcripts.md#drawn_morph) from the welcome screen's starting points and run `shapes`, then `paired`,
`morph` and `play`. To morph your own shapes, press `alt/option-d` and draw two closed strokes with the
pen (`p`), then replace `morphShapes()` in `shapes` with a line that names the two strokes you drew
last:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val mine = notation.strokes.filter { it.handDrawn }.takeLast(2)
notation.edit(mine[0]) { name = "from" }
notation.edit(mine[1]) { name = "to" }
```

Run the boxes after `shapes` again and they morph what you drew. A shape with corners, or two
shapes of very different sizes, makes the index-order fold worse.

# A Drawn Morph, Heard

Two strokes on the drawing layer, a circle and a heart. `notation` reads them back as lists of
points, `resampleByLength` gives each the same number of points, evenly spaced, and `matchPoints`
pairs every point of the circle with a point of the heart. Moving each point toward its partner is
a morph. The size of the cloud as it moves is a number per step, and played as pitch it is a tune
you can hear the shape change in.

The two strokes on this page are drawn by code, but two strokes you draw by hand and name "from" and
"to" are read the same way.

## Two strokes, paired

`morphShapes()` draws the circle in blue, starting on its right and going round anticlockwise, and
the heart in red, starting at its bottom point and going clockwise. The circle is drawn the way a
hand draws one, slowly off the start and into the end, so its points are bunched there. The box
reads both strokes back by name, resamples them, and matches them:

# Colors to FLine examples

*Every public declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference: [`colors.kt`](reference/graphics.md#colors-kt). Start from [what's already in the box](reference/index.md).*

This page builds palettes, sets of colors that have to work together on one drawing. Both examples draw the whole palette as geometry, because a drawing shows which entry is weak far sooner than a list of hex values does.

Every constructor returns an sRGB-encoded `Vec4` with components in `[0,1]`. There are four color spaces to build from:

- **sRGB**: `rgb(r, g, b, a)` (alias `rgba`) takes components already sRGB-encoded, on 0..1 or 0..255. The scale is guessed per call: any of `r`, `g`, `b` above 1 means 0..255. `rgb255(...)` is the same thing always on 0..255, so nothing is guessed.
- **HSL**: `hsl(h, s, l, a)` (alias `hsla`) is the classic cylinder, treated as linear light and then encoded to sRGB, so it is brighter than CSS `hsl()` at the same numbers.
- **OKHSL**: `okhsl(h, s, l, a)` is hue, saturation and lightness built on Oklab, with `l` as *perceived* lightness and `s = 1` at the gamut edge for that hue.
- **OKHSV**: `okhsv(h, s, v, a)` is the HSV-shaped version of the same, where `v` dims a color toward black.

The three hue-based spaces read `h` as a fraction of a turn below 1 and as degrees from 1 up. Each one also has a ring generator that spaces `count` hues evenly: `hueSetHsl`, `hueSetOkhsl` and `hueSetOkhsv`, with the short aliases `hslSet`, `okhslSet` and `okhsvSet`. `paletteForBackground` builds an OKHSL ring and then corrects it for contrast. Oklab itself is used inside the file and has no public constructor.

## HSL vs OKHSL hue sets

Stepping evenly round the hue wheel is the obvious way to ask for ten distinguishable colors, and it mostly works. What drifts is perceived weight. One swatch shouts, the next one disappears, and ten colors that were meant to read as a family stop doing so.

    val x1 = x0 + 78.0
    fline {

        lineTo(x1, y0)
        lineTo(x1, y0 + h)
        lineTo(x0, y0 + h)
        close()
        filled = true
        stroked = true
        color = c
        thickness = 1.2
    }

val okhslSet = hueSetOkhsl(10, saturation = 0.78, lightness = 0.58)

## paletteForBackground on layered paths

A palette can look fine in isolation and fail against a real background. The colors have to read against the ground and against each other, and on a dark canvas the ones that fail are the dark ones.

    for (i in 0..n) {

    filled = false
    this.color = color
    this.thickness = 3.0

![Seven nested rings in paletteForBackground colors on a dark background](assets/colors_examples/palette_background_paths.png)

Every ring stays readable and none sinks into the background. If nothing reaches `minContrast` the best candidate found is returned rather than an exception, so the call always hands back the count you asked for and it is the picture that tells you whether it managed. For more on constructing the underlying paths, see [FLine examples](fline_examples.md); for functional signal stacks that can drive color or geometry, see [Functions examples](functions_examples.md).

# Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments *Every public declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference: [`ValueVisualizer.kt`](reference/visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt), [`ImagingVisualizer.kt`](reference/visualization.md#imagingvisualizer-kt), [`plotly.kt`](reference/visualization.md#plotly-kt). Start from [what's already in the box](reference/index.md).* Field has many ways to show a value, and the quickest takes two keystrokes: put `.h` on the end of an expression and run the line. What comes back can land in several places. Some visuals appear **inline in the editor**, beside the line you ran. Some fill an **output area** under the box. Some output areas become **inspectors**, or **little control panels** whose sliders you drag while the code around them keeps running. And helpers like `.h` and `.h2` are about turning an arbitrary Kotlin value into something formatted well enough to read. This page is a tour of the whole family. ## The value visualizer: what `.h` draws Most environments answer "what is this value?" with a line of `toString()`. Field answers with a *picture*: whenever you ask Field to show a value, the **value visualizer** turns it into a compact HTML view — a reflective tree for arbitrary objects, and, for the types Field draws with, a little inline graphic. You reach it three ways, all of which call the same renderer (`ValueVisualizer.visualize(...)`, in `src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/ValueVisualizer.kt`): ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static value.h // the .h extension: value -> pretty HTML display("inspect", value.h) // drop that HTML into a named output channel box.viz(value = value) // convenience: visualize into the box's "viz" channel ``` `.h` is the lightweight view used throughout Field; its heavier sibling `.h2` opens a paged browser for large structures. The built-in and reflective paths are forgiving: they track recursion by reference, cap depth and preview sizes, catch reflective getter failures, and guard optional plots and thumbnails (including a throwing `Fn.evalFn`). Objects implementing `ToHTML` and callbacks registered with `registerValuePrinter` are extension points whose returned HTML is trusted. `registerValuePrinter` is how a **third-party** type joins in without knowing Field exists, and the worked example is a Kotlin DataFrame: a frame, a column, a row and a `GroupBy` all render as ordinary Field tables, and `.h2` pages a million-row frame through the same offset machinery this page's `.h2` uses everywhere else. See [DataFrames in a Box](dataframe.md#looking-at-a-frame). ### The reflective tree Give the visualizer an ordinary object — a data class, a map, anything with readable properties — and it walks the members into an indented tree. Numbers, booleans, strings, and nested values are each rendered by the same rules, recursively. ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static data class Camera( val position: Vector3f, val fieldOfView: Double, val active: Boolean, val layers: List ) val cam = Camera(Vector3f(0f, 1.5f, -4f), 55.0, true, ["dots", "lines", "labels"]) cam.h ``` ![Reflective tree for a Camera data class](assets/value_visualizers/reflective_tree.png){ width="516" } Notice that the tree is not flat text: the nested `position` is itself rendered as a `vec3`, and `layers` collapses to a list with a size count. The renderer keeps only a handful of fields inline (with a "… +N more fields" expander for the rest) so a large object never floods the output. ### Numeric collections, with stats Arrays and lists of numbers get a preview plus a one-line statistical summary — mean, standard deviation, and range — so you can judge a buffer without scrolling through it. Long collections elide the middle: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val samples = DoubleArray(48) { i -> sin(i / 48.0 * 2.0 * Math.PI) } samples.h ``` ![DoubleArray preview with mean, sigma and range](assets/value_visualizers/double_array.png) The tail reads `… +28 more items [μ=8.90e-17, σ=0.707, range=−1…1] (48)`: the sampled sine averages to ~0, has the expected 0.707 RMS spread, and spans −1…1 — visible immediately, without a plot. The same treatment applies to `IntArray`, `FloatArray`, and numeric `List`s. ### Vectors, matrices, and quaternions Field's generated linear-algebra types render as compact, colour-coded tokens rather than as reflective trees — the point of a `vec3` is its three numbers, not its class internals: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static [vec(0.5, 1.5), vec(1.0, 2.0, 3.0), vec(0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0)].h ``` ![vec2, vec3 and vec4 rendered as compact tokens](assets/value_visualizers/vectors.png){ width="324" } Matrices summarise rather than dump every cell: a `mat3` shows its determinant, a `mat4` shows determinant plus extracted translation, and a quaternion shows its four components. Here they are keyed by a map, which the visualizer renders as a tree — a good way to label several related values at once: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static linkedMapOf( "scale (mat3)" to Matrix3f().set(2f,0f,0f, 0f,3f,0f, 0f,0f,1f), "translate (mat4)" to Matrix4f().identity().apply { set(3,0,5f); set(3,1,-2f); set(3,2,1f) }, "spin (quat)" to Quaternionf().rotateY(0.6f) ).h ``` ![A map of mat3, mat4 and quaternion values](assets/value_visualizers/linalg_map.png){ width="564" } The `mat3` reports `det=6` (2 × 3 × 1), the `mat4` reports `det=1, t=(5, -2, 1)`, and the quaternion shows its normalized components. For the algebra behind these types, see [Linear Algebra](linear_algebra.md). ### An `FLine`, drawn An [`FLine`](fline_examples.md) — Field's core drawable path — is where the renderer stops summarising and starts *drawing*. Alongside its node counts, bounding box, length, and a compressed path signature, it appends a small inline SVG thumbnail of the actual geometry: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val spiral = FLine() val steps = 140 for (i in 0..steps) { val t = i.toDouble() / steps val a = t * 5.0 * 2.0 * Math.PI val r = 8.0 + t * 60.0 val x = 80.0 + Math.cos(a) * r val y = 80.0 + Math.sin(a) * r if (i == 0) spiral.moveTo(x, y) else spiral.lineTo(x, y) } spiral.h ``` ![FLine node stats, path signature, and an SVG spiral thumbnail](assets/value_visualizers/fline_spiral.png){ width="552" } The header reads `FLine (141 nodes)`, then `M=1 L=140 C=0 · b=130×124 · len=1.19e+03`, then the run-compressed signature `M(Lx41) … (Lx22)`, and finally the thumbnail. The thumbnail is normalised into its box and only rendered for paths under a complexity budget, so pasting a huge path into a value view never becomes a rendering hazard. ### An `Fn`, plotted The richest case is a [`Functions.Fn`](functions_examples.md). Field keeps the full reflective tree — its `domain`, `evalFn`, `graph`, and `name` — because that graph is the function's rebuildable structure. Then, below it, it appends a safe SVG line plot of the function sampled over a finite window of its domain: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static with(Functions) { val fn = sin(10) over (0.0..3.0) fn.h } ``` ![Fn reflective tree with an appended SVG sine plot](assets/value_visualizers/fn_sin_plot.png){ width="612" } The plot mirrors `Fn`'s own sampling rules: an unbounded domain falls back to a preview window, non-finite samples become gaps in the curve rather than spikes, a zero-straddling range draws a dashed baseline, and faint labels mark the value and domain extents (here `1.159 / −1.159` over `0 … 3`). If a function is non-finite everywhere, or its `evalFn` throws, the plot is simply omitted and the tree stands on its own — the value display is never allowed to fail. ### Images, edges, corners and flow The [imaging / computer-vision family](imaging_examples.md) gets the same treatment, and it is the case where the picture most obviously beats the text: an `Img` is a `FloatArray` you cannot read, a `List` is forty records of three doubles each, and a `GaussianPyramid` is `GaussianPyramid@3f1a2b`. Every imaging value below is rendered by `src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/ImagingVisualizer.kt`, reached through the same `.h` you have been using all along. Evaluate an `Img` and you get the actual pixels, aspect-correct, plus a `
` disclosure holding the per-channel strip, a per-channel histogram computed over the *full-resolution* samples, and the numbers: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val scene = Img.generateRGB(240, 180) { x, y -> /* … */ } scene.h ``` ![An RGB Img with its channel strip, histogram and statistics](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_rgb.png){ width="564" } #### The range policy This family is **float-channel and unbounded**. A Sobel `dx` is signed. An unnormalised response exceeds 1. An upstream division produces a NaN. A visualizer that just clamps everything to `0…1` answers all three questions with a flat white rectangle. So the renderer picks one of three modes and **always names the one it picked**: `direct` — every finite sample is already in `0…1`. Nothing is rescaled, and the caption says `direct`. That is the picture above. `signed ±m` — some sample is negative. The range is made symmetric about zero, so that *zero is a fixed, recognisable colour* rather than wherever `min…max` happened to put it, and a 1-channel image is run through the `coolwarm` diverging ramp from [`Colormaps`](rectsl_cheatsheet.md) — blue negative, pale zero, red positive. Grey simply cannot carry a sign: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static scene.luma().sobel().dx.h ``` ![A signed Sobel dx rendered with a coolwarm diverging map](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_signed_dx.png){ width="752" } Read it: the rectangle's left edge is red (dark→bright going right, so `dx > 0`) and its right edge is blue; the disc is warm on its left limb and cool on its right. `mean = 0.0002` and `σ = 0.052`, with the histogram spiking at zero, is what a gradient of a mostly-flat image should look like. The disclosure offers the same data read two more ways — plain `grey` and `viridis` — so you get three readings of one response image. `auto-ranged` — non-negative, but the maximum is above 1. Rescaled for display with the **true range printed**, so a bright pixel is never mistaken for 1.0: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static (scene.luma().sobelMagnitude() * 25f).h ``` ![An unnormalised response, auto-ranged with its true 0…10.26 range printed](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_autoranged.png){ width="752" } And non-finite samples — NaN, ±∞ — are counted, excluded from every statistic, and painted **magenta**: ![An image with a NaN block and one infinity, painted magenta](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_non_finite.png){ width="752" } Magenta because the alternative is silence: one NaN poisons `min()`/`max()`, `normalized()` returns an all-NaN image, and the PNG quantiser turns NaN into `0`, so a broken image comes back as an **all-black** thumbnail captioned `range NaN…NaN`. An image that is wrong should look wrong. Four-channel images sit on a checkerboard, so transparent black and opaque black are different pictures: ![An RGBA image over a checkerboard, with its alpha channel broken out](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_rgba.png){ width="732" } #### Gradients and pyramids A `Gradient` is two signed images and a direction, so it shows all of it — `dx`, `dy`, the magnitude, and the hue-by-direction image the type already knows how to build: ![A Gradient shown as dx, dy, magnitude and hue-by-direction](assets/imaging_visualizers/gradient.png){ width="752" } A pyramid is drawn as a **ladder of rungs at true relative scale**, bottom-aligned, so the halving is the visible fact rather than a number in a caption: ![A GaussianPyramid as five rungs at true relative scale](assets/imaging_visualizers/gaussian_pyramid.png){ width="752" } ![A LaplacianPyramid: signed band rungs plus a tagged residual](assets/imaging_visualizers/laplacian_pyramid.png){ width="752" } The Laplacian bands are signed, so they get the diverging treatment, and the one rung that is *not* a band is labelled `residual`. #### Detector output A `List` becomes a scatter with detector strength as both radius and `viridis` colour. A corner list carries no image extent, so the canvas is the points' own bounding box unioned with the origin — image coordinates start at `(0, 0)`, and including it keeps the points where they actually sit in the frame. The caption states the inferred extent: ![Harris corners as a strength-coded scatter](assets/imaging_visualizers/corners.png){ width="752" } The four strongest here read back as `(30.7, 26.7)`, `(89.3, 26.7)`, `(30.7, 75.3)`, `(89.3, 75.3)` — the four corners of a rectangle planted at `x 30…90, y 26…76` — and the single strongest is where the two rulings cross. A `HoughLine` is `(rho, theta)`: an **infinite** line with no extent of its own, which is why `toFLine` insists on being handed the image dimensions. With no image in reach the left panel clips each line into the smallest square every peak can still cross, says which square that was, and points at `linesToFLines` for the in-place version. The right panel needs no extent at all and is therefore exact: ρ against θ, sized by votes. ![Hough lines in an inferred square, beside their (theta, rho) accumulator peaks](assets/imaging_visualizers/hough_lines.png){ width="752" } A circle *does* have an extent, so no assumption is needed: ![Hough circles drawn over their own extent](assets/imaging_visualizers/hough_circles.png){ width="752" } A `FlowField` is a quiver — one arrow per converged track, hue by direction, and **failed tracks drawn as grey crosses** rather than dropped. A tracker that never reports failure is lying, and so is a picture that hides the failures. Displacements are drawn at true pixel scale unless the median motion is too small to see, in which case an integer exaggeration factor is applied and named: ![An optical-flow field as a hue-coded quiver, tracing a planted rotation](assets/imaging_visualizers/flow_field.png){ width="752" } The frames here differ by a 0.06 rad rotation about the centre, and that is exactly what the arrows trace: little motion near the middle, tangential motion at the edges, the hue rotating smoothly with the direction. Finally, a `ComponentLabelling` shows the label map under a golden-ratio hue rotation — adjacent label ids get unrelated colours, which is what makes two touching blobs distinguishable at thumbnail size — with the per-blob areas and centroids behind the disclosure: ![A connected-component label map with one hue per blob](assets/imaging_visualizers/components.png){ width="752" } A plain `List` becomes a filmstrip, which is the shape a frame sequence or a parameter sweep already has: ![A List as a filmstrip of a blur sweep](assets/imaging_visualizers/filmstrip.png){ width="752" } #### All of it, in a real box Everything above is a fragment rendered on its own. Here is the same renderer inside an actual Field box, in Field's own output areas: a whole pipeline, with `.h` doing all the work. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-imaging-panels.png" alt="four imaging panels in a row, each a thumbnail over a line of metadata and a row of disclosure links. An RGB image of a yellow rectangle and a cyan disc on a four-way colour gradient, labelled 180x132, rgb, range 0.1 to 0.98; a signed Sobel response of the same scene painted in the blue-white-red coolwarm map, labelled range -0.4083 to 0.4089, signed; a GaussianPyramid as four rungs at true relative scale, 180x132 down to 22x16; and a List of 9 Corners as coloured dots on black, labelled with its response range and an inferred extent of 118.23 by 106.17" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="8" w="1200" h="700" embed=true name="imaging-panels"} :::static val scene = Img.generateRGB(180, 132) { x, y -> var r = 0.10f + 0.30f * (x / 179f) var g = 0.12f + 0.22f * (y / 131f) var b = 0.34f - 0.20f * (x / 179f) if (x in 24..68 && y in 20..56) { r = 0.94f; g = 0.86f; b = 0.42f } if (hypot(x - 128.0, y - 46.0) <= 22.0) { r = 0.30f; g = 0.80f; b = 0.92f } if (x in 112..113 || y in 104..105) { r = 0.98f; g = 0.98f; b = 0.98f } Triple(r, g, b) } val gray = scene.luma() // Four stages of one pipeline, four different value types, one `.h` each. showRow keeps // them in a single output channel instead of four tall ones. val panels = [ scene.h, // direct mode, 3 channels gray.sobel().dx.h, // signed -> coolwarm diverging gray.gaussianPyramid(4).h, // rungs at true relative scale gray.harrisCorners(minDistance = 6, maxCount = 20).h // scatter, strength-coded ] showRow("panels", panels) println("imaging visualizers ready") ``` Note what is *not* in that code: no `showImg`, no PNG encoding, no colour-map choice, no normalisation, no per-type branching. `.h` is the whole interface, and the renderer decides per value whether it is looking at colour data, a signed response, a pyramid, or a list of detections. !!! tip "Open the demo document" The [imaging_visualizers_demo](agent_transcripts.md#imaging_visualizers_demo) starting point has one box per visualizer on this page. Open it from the welcome screen, run the boxes and look at each one's output area — every box evaluates one imaging value as its last expression, so there is no `showImg`, no `display(...)` and no explicit call at all. Then change a sigma or a threshold and re-run a box. The rest of this page is the *instruments* built on top of this renderer: inline probes that live next to a line of code, display channels, control surfaces, and synth scopes. ## Inline editor visualizers These draw next to the line of code that produced the value. The core pattern is: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val m = __m("some-marker") m.histogram(0.42) ``` The marker remembers a little state and renders HTML back into the editor gutter / inline output location for that line. ### Histogram, history, and summary stats Histograms answer “what values have I seen?”, history answers “how did the value move?”, and stats gives you a one-line summary. The live examples below are all `loop { }` bodies, which is Field's frame loop: the body runs, then the frame advances, once per Runloop tick. What that tick is, and what stops one of these, is [Frames and the animation loop](animation_time_model.md). ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-metrics.mp4" wait="1.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-metrics"} :::static var tick = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 println("inline metrics ready") loop { tick += 0.4 visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { val value = sin(tick * 0.22) * 0.7 + cos(tick * 0.11) * 0.2 + tick * 0.01 __m("histogram").histogram(value, dur = 120) __m("trail").history(value, dur = 48) __m("summary").stats(value, dur = 48) } frame() } ``` Those three calls all share the same basic idea: - `ᛟ.histogram(value)` keeps a rolling distribution. - `ᛟ.history(value)` keeps a rolling time series. - `ᛟ.stats(value)` gives a compact summary panel. In the editor you can add a marker rune (ᛟ), with f1, "Insert Stack Mark", or shift+command period: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin capture="ui" region="window" clip-selector=".afield-palette-shell" screenshot="assets/insert-stack-mark.png" alt="Insert stack mark command" padding="6" wait="0" timeout="90" embed=true hidden=true name="insert-stack-mark"} ui.openEditor(id) ui.pause(700) ui.waitForSelector(".monaco-editor", 15000.0) ui.clickSelector(".monaco-editor") ui.pause(300) ui.press("F1") ui.waitForSelector(".afield-palette-shell", 8000.0) ui.pause(400) ui.type("stack") ui.pause(1200) ``` These functions are **passthroughs**. They return the value they were given, so you can drop them into a chain when you want to inspect the value flowing through a wire without changing the computation: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val filtered = __m("cutoff").history(rawCutoff) ``` That makes them excellent debugging instruments: tiny scopes for values, not transformations of values. If you want a **live** feed rather than a one-shot summary, write a loop and **launch** the box: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-live-history.mp4" wait="2.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-live-history"} :::static println("live history launched") var phase = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 loop { visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { val y = sin(phase * 0.8) + 0.2 * sin(phase * 7.0) __m("live").history(y, dur = 120) } phase += 0.07 frame() } ``` The same loop is shorter written against the box's `time` instead of a phase it advances itself: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static loop { val t = time val y = sin(t * 0.8) + 0.2 * sin(t * 7.0) __m("live").history(y, dur = 120) frame() } ``` Run either as a launch, not a plain execute. ### Piano rolls in the editor The piano-roll visualizer is the same idea, but for scheduled notes rather than scalar values. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-pianoroll.mp4" wait="2.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-pianoroll"} :::static val arp = noteProcess { val chord = [48, 55, 60, 64] var step = 0 while (true) { note( pitch = chord[step % chord.size], duration = 0.18, velocity = 0.85, label = "n$step" ) rest(0.25) step++ } } println("inline piano roll launched") var playhead = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 loop { visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { __m("arp").pianoRoll(arp.at(playhead)) } playhead += 0.35 frame() } ``` Use it for sequencers, generative rhythm systems, or anything where you want to see future note structure without leaving the code. ## Display channels: the big canvas under the box Inline visuals sit beside one line of code. `display(...)` has the whole area under the box. Anything you pass to `display("channel", thing)` becomes HTML in a named output area. That HTML can be handwritten, auto-generated, interactive, or even an embedded browser/inspector. ### Raw HTML, pretty HTML, and heavy HTML - `display("channel", "

Use `.h2` when you want to browse instead of read. That covers a large map, list, array or buffer without turning the output area into soup, and it covers your own data classes and Field's own types too. `.h2` on a plain object gives you its properties as a scrollable table: one row per property, with its declared type and its value. Above the table sit `outliner` and `columns` links, which open the same value in the full tree and column browsers. There is nothing to register; it reflects. If a property's getter throws, the row is still there, marked, with the exception text in its value cell. Four things are special-cased, because their fields are not where the interesting content is. A `Box` shows its name, frame, code size, run state, its whole property bag, and a table of its `parents`, `children`, `nested` and `nestedIn` edges. An `Fn` shows a sampled table of `x` and `f(x)` across its domain, because a function is its values and its one substantive field is a private closure. An `FLine` shows its node table: instruction kind, control-point count and endpoint per row. An exception shows its message, its cause chain and its stack. Some values `.h2` hands straight back to `.h`, because the compact rendering already *is* the value: numbers, strings, enums, a `Pair`, a vector, a matrix (which `.h` draws as a heatmap), and a `Quantity`, whose whole point is a number next to a unit. To see all of it at once, insert the **h2 Explorer Examples** template and run its boxes top to bottom. ### Markdown for captions and tables The escape hatch above has a way of taking over. A figure that wants a heading, a key/value table and a block of computed text ends up as a hundred lines of string concatenation, with a hand-picked font stack, a `` builder and a local `fun esc(s: String)`, often longer than the code it illustrates. `markdown("channel", "…")` says the same thing in markdown, and picks up Field's own `--field-*` tokens instead of re-inventing them: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-markdown.png" alt="one markdown card headed 'what the run settled on'. A two-column reading/value table gives tempo 122, drift -0.004 and voice 'saw 110 *'. Under it a status line reads stable, budget 83% used in amber, no retries. Then a two-column row labelled BEFORE and AFTER, holding gain 0.2 on the left and gain 0.9 on the right, and a quoted solver-output block reading 'converged in 41 steps, residual 3.2e-7'" wait="2.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="900" embed=true name="display-markdown"} :::static val readings = linkedMapOf("tempo" to 122, "drift" to -0.004, "voice" to "saw 110 *") val rows = readings.entries.joinToString("\n") { (k, v) -> "| ${k.md} | ${v.md} |" } val report = "converged in 41 steps\nresidual 3.2e-7" markdown("figure", """ ### what the run settled on | reading | value | |---------|-------| $rows status: {ok:**stable**} · budget: {warn:83% used} · {muted:no retries} :::row #### before ${mapOf("gain" to 0.2).h} --- #### after ${mapOf("gain" to 0.9).h} :::end #### solver output ~~~ $report ~~~ """, width = 820) println("markdown figure ready") ``` Three rules matter once a figure mixes computed values into the prose: - **HTML passes through, inline and block.** `.h`, `diffHtml()`, `graphSvg()` and friends already return HTML; interpolate them directly and they land verbatim, table cells included. Only text you actually wrote as markdown gets escaped. - **`value.md` for computed values.** Runtime values are not markdown — a `|` splits the row it lands in, a pair of `*` becomes emphasis, a `` is read as a tag and vanishes. Escape anything you did not write yourself. `mdEscape(value)` is the same function, written as a call. - **Fenced bodies are interpolated at column zero**, hard left, the way `$report` is above. Inside a fence whitespace is the content, and splicing at the surrounding indentation would indent only the value's first line. Beyond GitHub-flavoured markdown there are two additions: `:::row … :::end`, splitting columns on a `---` line, for the before/after shape markdown cannot spell; and `{role:text}` spans — `accent`, `muted`, `dim`, `ok`, `warn`, `bad` — so a callout never needs a hex literal. Neither applies inside code, so a `:::row` or a `{warn:…}` shown *as* an example stays as written. The figure above uses both: the before/after row, and the `ok`, `warn` and `muted` spans on its status line. You do not need `trimIndent()`; the text is dedented for you, and unlike `trimIndent` it survives having a multi-line value interpolated into it. `width` pins the card's width; without it the card is as wide as its widest unbreakable line. ### Trees and columns For a value you want to browse like a little filesystem, open it in a tree or column browser. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-display-browsers.png" alt="two inspector channels over the same nested scene map. 'outline' is a tree browser with camera expanded to show x, y, zoom and active, and layers and palette still folded. 'columns' is a column browser, its root column listing camera, layers and palette with a scrollbar down the right of the pane" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1200" h="260" embed=true name="display-browsers"} :::static val scene = linkedMapOf( "camera" to linkedMapOf( "x" to 10, "y" to 20, "zoom" to 1.5, "active" to true ), "layers" to [ linkedMapOf( "name" to "dots", "visible" to true, "points" to [2, 4, 8, 16] ), linkedMapOf( "name" to "lines", "visible" to false, "style" to linkedMapOf("width" to 2, "color" to "#f2aa4c") ) ], "palette" to linkedMapOf( "background" to "#101820", "accent" to "#f2aa4c" ) ) tree("outline", scene) column("columns", scene) println("inspector panes ready") ``` - `tree("channel", value)` gives you an outline / tree browser. - `column("channel", value)` gives you a column-style browser. These are especially good for nested maps, scene graphs, structured JSON-like data, or anything you want to poke around in rather than summarize. Both take any value, not only maps and lists. A data class or one of your own classes opens to its public properties, an `IntArray` or `DoubleArray` opens to its elements, and a map whose keys are objects opens each entry to its key and its value. Every row shows its name, its type and a one-line summary (`5000 items`, `"label"`, `Point(x=1.0, y=2.5, label=p)`), so you can read most of a structure without opening anything: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-tree-values.png" alt="A tree embed titled LinkedHashMap, 4 entries, with a filter box. A plain drag works like `vec2Control(...)`, and the callback gets each position. **Shift-drag** records a take: the whole stroke and its timing, kept with the box like any other control value. On a phone, tap **rec**, then draw. The trail of the take stays on the pad. The box replays the take, and the box keeps the time. `at(seconds)` returns where the take is that far into its loop, interpolated between the recorded samples, and `playhead(seconds)` puts a ring on the pad there. Read both off the clock in a `loop`, as the sequencer does, and the replay never drifts and keeps going with the browser closed. `initialTake` gives the pad something to play before you have recorded anything; here it is a figure eight: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-gesture.mp4" capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait-output="true" wait-output-kind="display" execution="launch" duration="4" fps="20" timeout="180" w="600" embed=true name="gesture" alt="an XY pad headed MOVE with the readout 2.0 s take and a rec button. Use `polar = true` when the value wraps around, like a phase or a hue. - Use `menu(...)` for choosing one of a few named options. - Use `gesture(...)` for a two-axis movement you want to perform once and loop. - For a curve over time you shape by hand, an envelope, use the keyframe editor, `keyframes(...)`: see [Keyframes and timelines](funFeatures.md#keyframes-and-timelines). It combines a waveform and native browser audio controls, keeps an optional vertical playhead synchronized with playback, and uses the waveform itself as a navigator: - click to seek; - drag to pan; - use the mouse wheel or `+` / `−` to zoom while keeping the visible playhead fixed on screen; - shift-wheel to pan; - double-click or press **all** to restore the complete clip. If the playhead is outside the visible interval, wheel zoom falls back to the pointer and button or keyboard zoom falls back to the center. Near the start or end of a recording, boundary clamping may move the playhead on screen. A completion-style spinner remains over the waveform while a newly zoomed or panned min/max envelope is loading, so the old waveform cannot be mistaken for the new view. During playback, crossing the right edge advances the visible interval and places the playhead slightly inside the new window; crossing the left edge after a backward seek mirrors that behavior. Set `followPlayhead = false` in `AudioVisualizerOptions` to keep a zoomed interval stationary. Waveform-envelope requests have a 15-second browser deadline; a stalled service clears the spinner and reports a timeout instead of leaving the view permanently busy. For a Field Audio service representation, use the same component without transferring or decoding the complete recording just to draw it: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} val representation: AssetRepresentation = candidate.proxyRepresentation!! display("audio", representation.audioVisualizerHtml( options = AudioVisualizerOptions(showPlayhead = true) )) ``` That adapter asks the service for a bounded min/max envelope of only the visible interval. Each source frame contributes to a pixel's minimum or maximum, preserving short transients that simple sample decimation would miss. Zooming and panning request a new envelope with at most 4096 points; the audio itself continues to stream from the immutable representation. Set `showPlayhead = false` for a waveform-only inspection surface. ### Shared time cursors and transport Audio players and arbitrary time-based views can share a loose, browser-side timeline. A component whose local zero is later on the source timeline also gets an offset; shared time is always `localSeconds + syncOffsetSeconds`. ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} val group = "nancy-analysis" display("source", representation.audioVisualizerHtml( options = AudioVisualizerOptions( initialStartSeconds = 18.0, initialDurationSeconds = 24.0, initialPositionSeconds = 18.0, syncGroup = group, ) )) // Analysis-local 0 s corresponds to source 18 s. display("analysis", analysisDashboardHtml( [beats, mono, poly], syncGroup = group, timeOffsetSeconds = 18.0, )) ``` This synchronizes across separate `display(...)` output documents. The audio pane draws the decaying 220 Hz ping as a cyan waveform above a browser transport parked at 0:00 of 0:02, its chip reading click seek, wheel zoom at playhead, drag pan. For the function it is `1024/1024 samples` until you zoom inside the domain, and then `live · Δx …`, because `Fn.plot` resamples the function as you zoom. For the signal it is the sampling grid, `envelope · Δt …` or `waveform · Δt …`. The strip under each plot is the whole domain. It stays dim until you zoom, then marks the visible window; click or drag it to move. The ripple in the white band is the signal's sampling grid showing through: at this zoom each bin holds about ten samples, roughly a third of a 220 Hz cycle, so a bin's min and max rarely land on a peak. Per-job progress can replace a named output with `fieldAudioJobStatusHtml(accepted, event)`, while `fieldAudioJobMonitor()` embeds the complete durable queue. A strip underneath shows WebRTC voice activity, dBFS energy, and embedding novelty. Give the source `AudioVisualizer` and the speech view the same `syncGroup`. Audio playback moves a marker through both portraits; hovering either portrait publishes the nearest frame time; clicking seeks the player. The view also listens to `field-time-window`, so the waveform's visible interval stays saturated while the rest of the embedding path recedes. 'audio' pairs a dense stereo waveform at peak 0.858, rms 0.382 with a spectrum whose harmonics march up to a broad shelf past 5 kHz. 'scope' shows the same pair after filtering: a smaller waveform at peak 0.355 and a spectrum whose partials die away by 5 kHz. 'env' draws an ADSR, the orange gate dropping partway across and the blue level decaying after it, tagged RELEASE, lvl 0.401. So the choice is mostly about **where you want the visual to live**. ## Choosing between inline and display Here is the practical rule of thumb: - If the visual explains one line of code, put it inline on a stack mark (ᛟ, **Insert Stack Mark**). - If the visual explains a whole box or deserves interaction, put it in `display(...)`. - If the thing is large and structural, use `tree(...)`, `column(...)`, or `.h2`. - If the thing is tiny and human-readable, `.h` is often perfect. `histogram(...)` and `history(...)` return the value they were given, so you can leave them in a computation while you debug it. All of these tools compose. One box can have a little inline history, a piano roll, a browser in one output channel, and a control surface in another. Field is very happy when code is also an interface.

# Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments *Every public declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference: [`ValueVisualizer.kt`](reference/visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt), [`ImagingVisualizer.kt`](reference/visualization.md#imagingvisualizer-kt), [`plotly.kt`](reference/visualization.md#plotly-kt). Start from [what's already in the box](reference/index.md).* Field has many ways to show a value, and the quickest takes two keystrokes: put `.h` on the end of an expression and run the line. What comes back can land in several places. Some visuals appear **inline in the editor**, beside the line you ran. Some fill an **output area** under the box. Some output areas become **inspectors**, or **little control panels** whose sliders you drag while the code around them keeps running. And helpers like `.h` and `.h2` are about turning an arbitrary Kotlin value into something formatted well enough to read. This page is a tour of the whole family. ## The value visualizer: what `.h` draws Most environments answer "what is this value?" with a line of `toString()`. Field answers with a *picture*: whenever you ask Field to show a value, the **value visualizer** turns it into a compact HTML view — a reflective tree for arbitrary objects, and, for the types Field draws with, a little inline graphic. You reach it three ways, all of which call the same renderer (`ValueVisualizer.visualize(...)`, in `src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/ValueVisualizer.kt`): ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static value.h // the .h extension: value -> pretty HTML display("inspect", value.h) // drop that HTML into a named output channel box.viz(value = value) // convenience: visualize into the box's "viz" channel ``` `.h` is the lightweight view used throughout Field; its heavier sibling `.h2` opens a paged browser for large structures. The built-in and reflective paths are forgiving: they track recursion by reference, cap depth and preview sizes, catch reflective getter failures, and guard optional plots and thumbnails (including a throwing `Fn.evalFn`). Objects implementing `ToHTML` and callbacks registered with `registerValuePrinter` are extension points whose returned HTML is trusted. `registerValuePrinter` is how a **third-party** type joins in without knowing Field exists, and the worked example is a Kotlin DataFrame: a frame, a column, a row and a `GroupBy` all render as ordinary Field tables, and `.h2` pages a million-row frame through the same offset machinery this page's `.h2` uses everywhere else. See [DataFrames in a Box](dataframe.md#looking-at-a-frame). ### The reflective tree Give the visualizer an ordinary object — a data class, a map, anything with readable properties — and it walks the members into an indented tree. Numbers, booleans, strings, and nested values are each rendered by the same rules, recursively. ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static data class Camera( val position: Vector3f, val fieldOfView: Double, val active: Boolean, val layers: List ) val cam = Camera(Vector3f(0f, 1.5f, -4f), 55.0, true, ["dots", "lines", "labels"]) cam.h ``` ![Reflective tree for a Camera data class](assets/value_visualizers/reflective_tree.png){ width="516" } Notice that the tree is not flat text: the nested `position` is itself rendered as a `vec3`, and `layers` collapses to a list with a size count. The renderer keeps only a handful of fields inline (with a "… +N more fields" expander for the rest) so a large object never floods the output. ### Numeric collections, with stats Arrays and lists of numbers get a preview plus a one-line statistical summary — mean, standard deviation, and range — so you can judge a buffer without scrolling through it. Long collections elide the middle: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val samples = DoubleArray(48) { i -> sin(i / 48.0 * 2.0 * Math.PI) } samples.h ``` ![DoubleArray preview with mean, sigma and range](assets/value_visualizers/double_array.png) The tail reads `… +28 more items [μ=8.90e-17, σ=0.707, range=−1…1] (48)`: the sampled sine averages to ~0, has the expected 0.707 RMS spread, and spans −1…1 — visible immediately, without a plot. The same treatment applies to `IntArray`, `FloatArray`, and numeric `List`s. ### Vectors, matrices, and quaternions Field's generated linear-algebra types render as compact, colour-coded tokens rather than as reflective trees — the point of a `vec3` is its three numbers, not its class internals: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static [vec(0.5, 1.5), vec(1.0, 2.0, 3.0), vec(0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0)].h ``` ![vec2, vec3 and vec4 rendered as compact tokens](assets/value_visualizers/vectors.png){ width="324" } Matrices summarise rather than dump every cell: a `mat3` shows its determinant, a `mat4` shows determinant plus extracted translation, and a quaternion shows its four components. Here they are keyed by a map, which the visualizer renders as a tree — a good way to label several related values at once: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static linkedMapOf( "scale (mat3)" to Matrix3f().set(2f,0f,0f, 0f,3f,0f, 0f,0f,1f), "translate (mat4)" to Matrix4f().identity().apply { set(3,0,5f); set(3,1,-2f); set(3,2,1f) }, "spin (quat)" to Quaternionf().rotateY(0.6f) ).h ``` ![A map of mat3, mat4 and quaternion values](assets/value_visualizers/linalg_map.png){ width="564" } The `mat3` reports `det=6` (2 × 3 × 1), the `mat4` reports `det=1, t=(5, -2, 1)`, and the quaternion shows its normalized components. For the algebra behind these types, see [Linear Algebra](linear_algebra.md). ### An `FLine`, drawn An [`FLine`](fline_examples.md) — Field's core drawable path — is where the renderer stops summarising and starts *drawing*. Alongside its node counts, bounding box, length, and a compressed path signature, it appends a small inline SVG thumbnail of the actual geometry: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val spiral = FLine() val steps = 140 spiral.breakNext() for (i in 0..steps) { val t = i.toDouble() / steps val a = t * 5.0 * 2.0 * Math.PI val r = 8.0 + t * 60.0 val x = 80.0 + Math.cos(a) * r val y = 80.0 + Math.sin(a) * r spiral.lineTo(x, y) } spiral.h ``` ![FLine node stats, path signature, and an SVG spiral thumbnail](assets/value_visualizers/fline_spiral.png){ width="552" } The header reads `FLine (141 nodes)`, then `M=1 L=140 C=0 · b=130×124 · len=1.19e+03`, then the run-compressed signature `M(Lx41) … (Lx22)`, and finally the thumbnail. The thumbnail is normalised into its box and only rendered for paths under a complexity budget, so pasting a huge path into a value view never becomes a rendering hazard. ### An `Fn`, plotted The richest case is a [`Functions.Fn`](functions_examples.md). Field keeps the full reflective tree — its `domain`, `evalFn`, `graph`, and `name` — because that graph is the function's rebuildable structure. Then, below it, it appends a safe SVG line plot of the function sampled over a finite window of its domain: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static with(Functions) { val fn = sin(10) over (0.0..3.0) fn.h } ``` ![Fn reflective tree with an appended SVG sine plot](assets/value_visualizers/fn_sin_plot.png){ width="612" } The plot mirrors `Fn`'s own sampling rules: an unbounded domain falls back to a preview window, non-finite samples become gaps in the curve rather than spikes, a zero-straddling range draws a dashed baseline, and faint labels mark the value and domain extents (here `1.159 / −1.159` over `0 … 3`). If a function is non-finite everywhere, or its `evalFn` throws, the plot is simply omitted and the tree stands on its own — the value display is never allowed to fail. ### Images, edges, corners and flow The [imaging / computer-vision family](imaging_examples.md) gets the same treatment, and it is the case where the picture most obviously beats the text: an `Img` is a `FloatArray` you cannot read, a `List` is forty records of three doubles each, and a `GaussianPyramid` is `GaussianPyramid@3f1a2b`. Every imaging value below is rendered by `src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/ImagingVisualizer.kt`, reached through the same `.h` you have been using all along. Evaluate an `Img` and you get the actual pixels, aspect-correct, plus a `
` disclosure holding the per-channel strip, a per-channel histogram computed over the *full-resolution* samples, and the numbers: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val scene = Img.generateRGB(240, 180) { x, y -> /* … */ } scene.h ``` ![An RGB Img with its channel strip, histogram and statistics](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_rgb.png){ width="564" } #### The range policy This family is **float-channel and unbounded**. A Sobel `dx` is signed. An unnormalised response exceeds 1. An upstream division produces a NaN. A visualizer that just clamps everything to `0…1` answers all three questions with a flat white rectangle. So the renderer picks one of three modes and **always names the one it picked**: `direct` — every finite sample is already in `0…1`. Nothing is rescaled, and the caption says `direct`. That is the picture above. `signed ±m` — some sample is negative. The range is made symmetric about zero, so that *zero is a fixed, recognisable colour* rather than wherever `min…max` happened to put it, and a 1-channel image is run through the `coolwarm` diverging ramp from [`Colormaps`](rectsl_cheatsheet.md) — blue negative, pale zero, red positive. Grey simply cannot carry a sign: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static scene.luma().sobel().dx.h ``` ![A signed Sobel dx rendered with a coolwarm diverging map](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_signed_dx.png){ width="752" } Read it: the rectangle's left edge is red (dark→bright going right, so `dx > 0`) and its right edge is blue; the disc is warm on its left limb and cool on its right. `mean = 0.0002` and `σ = 0.052`, with the histogram spiking at zero, is what a gradient of a mostly-flat image should look like. The disclosure offers the same data read two more ways — plain `grey` and `viridis` — so you get three readings of one response image. `auto-ranged` — non-negative, but the maximum is above 1. Rescaled for display with the **true range printed**, so a bright pixel is never mistaken for 1.0: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static (scene.luma().sobelMagnitude() * 25f).h ``` ![An unnormalised response, auto-ranged with its true 0…10.26 range printed](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_autoranged.png){ width="752" } And non-finite samples — NaN, ±∞ — are counted, excluded from every statistic, and painted **magenta**: ![An image with a NaN block and one infinity, painted magenta](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_non_finite.png){ width="752" } Magenta because the alternative is silence: one NaN poisons `min()`/`max()`, `normalized()` returns an all-NaN image, and the PNG quantiser turns NaN into `0`, so a broken image comes back as an **all-black** thumbnail captioned `range NaN…NaN`. An image that is wrong should look wrong. Four-channel images sit on a checkerboard, so transparent black and opaque black are different pictures: ![An RGBA image over a checkerboard, with its alpha channel broken out](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_rgba.png){ width="732" } #### Gradients and pyramids A `Gradient` is two signed images and a direction, so it shows all of it — `dx`, `dy`, the magnitude, and the hue-by-direction image the type already knows how to build: ![A Gradient shown as dx, dy, magnitude and hue-by-direction](assets/imaging_visualizers/gradient.png){ width="752" } A pyramid is drawn as a **ladder of rungs at true relative scale**, bottom-aligned, so the halving is the visible fact rather than a number in a caption: ![A GaussianPyramid as five rungs at true relative scale](assets/imaging_visualizers/gaussian_pyramid.png){ width="752" } ![A LaplacianPyramid: signed band rungs plus a tagged residual](assets/imaging_visualizers/laplacian_pyramid.png){ width="752" } The Laplacian bands are signed, so they get the diverging treatment, and the one rung that is *not* a band is labelled `residual`. #### Detector output A `List` becomes a scatter with detector strength as both radius and `viridis` colour. A corner list carries no image extent, so the canvas is the points' own bounding box unioned with the origin — image coordinates start at `(0, 0)`, and including it keeps the points where they actually sit in the frame. The caption states the inferred extent: ![Harris corners as a strength-coded scatter](assets/imaging_visualizers/corners.png){ width="752" } The four strongest here read back as `(30.7, 26.7)`, `(89.3, 26.7)`, `(30.7, 75.3)`, `(89.3, 75.3)` — the four corners of a rectangle planted at `x 30…90, y 26…76` — and the single strongest is where the two rulings cross. A `HoughLine` is `(rho, theta)`: an **infinite** line with no extent of its own, which is why `toFLine` insists on being handed the image dimensions. With no image in reach the left panel clips each line into the smallest square every peak can still cross, says which square that was, and points at `linesToFLines` for the in-place version. The right panel needs no extent at all and is therefore exact: ρ against θ, sized by votes. ![Hough lines in an inferred square, beside their (theta, rho) accumulator peaks](assets/imaging_visualizers/hough_lines.png){ width="752" } A circle *does* have an extent, so no assumption is needed: ![Hough circles drawn over their own extent](assets/imaging_visualizers/hough_circles.png){ width="752" } A `FlowField` is a quiver — one arrow per converged track, hue by direction, and **failed tracks drawn as grey crosses** rather than dropped. A tracker that never reports failure is lying, and so is a picture that hides the failures. Displacements are drawn at true pixel scale unless the median motion is too small to see, in which case an integer exaggeration factor is applied and named: ![An optical-flow field as a hue-coded quiver, tracing a planted rotation](assets/imaging_visualizers/flow_field.png){ width="752" } The frames here differ by a 0.06 rad rotation about the centre, and that is exactly what the arrows trace: little motion near the middle, tangential motion at the edges, the hue rotating smoothly with the direction. Finally, a `ComponentLabelling` shows the label map under a golden-ratio hue rotation — adjacent label ids get unrelated colours, which is what makes two touching blobs distinguishable at thumbnail size — with the per-blob areas and centroids behind the disclosure: ![A connected-component label map with one hue per blob](assets/imaging_visualizers/components.png){ width="752" } A plain `List` becomes a filmstrip, which is the shape a frame sequence or a parameter sweep already has: ![A List as a filmstrip of a blur sweep](assets/imaging_visualizers/filmstrip.png){ width="752" } #### All of it, in a real box Everything above is a fragment rendered on its own. Here is the same renderer inside an actual Field box, in Field's own output areas: a whole pipeline, with `.h` doing all the work. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-imaging-panels.png" alt="four imaging panels in a row, each a thumbnail over a line of metadata and a row of disclosure links. An RGB image of a yellow rectangle and a cyan disc on a four-way colour gradient, labelled 180x132, rgb, range 0.1 to 0.98; a signed Sobel response of the same scene painted in the blue-white-red coolwarm map, labelled range -0.4083 to 0.4089, signed; a GaussianPyramid as four rungs at true relative scale, 180x132 down to 22x16; and a List of 9 Corners as coloured dots on black, labelled with its response range and an inferred extent of 118.23 by 106.17" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="8" w="1200" h="700" embed=true name="imaging-panels"} :::static val scene = Img.generateRGB(180, 132) { x, y -> var r = 0.10f + 0.30f * (x / 179f) var g = 0.12f + 0.22f * (y / 131f) var b = 0.34f - 0.20f * (x / 179f) if (x in 24..68 && y in 20..56) { r = 0.94f; g = 0.86f; b = 0.42f } if (hypot(x - 128.0, y - 46.0) <= 22.0) { r = 0.30f; g = 0.80f; b = 0.92f } if (x in 112..113 || y in 104..105) { r = 0.98f; g = 0.98f; b = 0.98f } Triple(r, g, b) } val gray = scene.luma() // Four stages of one pipeline, four different value types, one `.h` each. showRow keeps // them in a single output channel instead of four tall ones. val panels = [ scene.h, // direct mode, 3 channels gray.sobel().dx.h, // signed -> coolwarm diverging gray.gaussianPyramid(4).h, // rungs at true relative scale gray.harrisCorners(minDistance = 6, maxCount = 20).h // scatter, strength-coded ] showRow("panels", panels) println("imaging visualizers ready") ``` Note what is *not* in that code: no `showImg`, no PNG encoding, no colour-map choice, no normalisation, no per-type branching. `.h` is the whole interface, and the renderer decides per value whether it is looking at colour data, a signed response, a pyramid, or a list of detections. !!! tip "Open the demo document" The [imaging_visualizers_demo](agent_transcripts.md#imaging_visualizers_demo) starting point has one box per visualizer on this page. Open it from the welcome screen, run the boxes and look at each one's output area — every box evaluates one imaging value as its last expression, so there is no `showImg`, no `display(...)` and no explicit call at all. Then change a sigma or a threshold and re-run a box. The rest of this page is the *instruments* built on top of this renderer: inline probes that live next to a line of code, display channels, control surfaces, and synth scopes. ## Inline editor visualizers These draw next to the line of code that produced the value. The core pattern is: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val m = __m("some-marker") m.histogram(0.42) ``` The marker remembers a little state and renders HTML back into the editor gutter / inline output location for that line. ### Histogram, history, and summary stats Histograms answer “what values have I seen?”, history answers “how did the value move?”, and stats gives you a one-line summary. The live examples below are all `loop { }` bodies, which is Field's frame loop: the body runs, then the frame advances, once per Runloop tick. What that tick is, and what stops one of these, is [Frames and the animation loop](animation_time_model.md). ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-metrics.mp4" wait="1.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-metrics"} :::static var tick = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 println("inline metrics ready") loop { tick += 0.4 visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { val value = sin(tick * 0.22) * 0.7 + cos(tick * 0.11) * 0.2 + tick * 0.01 __m("histogram").histogram(value, dur = 120) __m("trail").history(value, dur = 48) __m("summary").stats(value, dur = 48) } frame() } ``` Those three calls all share the same basic idea: - `ᛟ.histogram(value)` keeps a rolling distribution. - `ᛟ.history(value)` keeps a rolling time series. - `ᛟ.stats(value)` gives a compact summary panel. In the editor you can add a marker rune (ᛟ), with f1, "Insert Stack Mark", or shift+command period: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin capture="ui" region="window" clip-selector=".afield-palette-shell" screenshot="assets/insert-stack-mark.png" alt="Insert stack mark command" padding="6" wait="0" timeout="90" embed=true hidden=true name="insert-stack-mark"} ui.openEditor(id) ui.pause(700) ui.waitForSelector(".monaco-editor", 15000.0) ui.clickSelector(".monaco-editor") ui.pause(300) ui.press("F1") ui.waitForSelector(".afield-palette-shell", 8000.0) ui.pause(400) ui.type("stack") ui.pause(1200) ``` These functions are **passthroughs**. They return the value they were given, so you can drop them into a chain when you want to inspect the value flowing through a wire without changing the computation: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val filtered = __m("cutoff").history(rawCutoff) ``` That makes them excellent debugging instruments: tiny scopes for values, not transformations of values. If you want a **live** feed rather than a one-shot summary, write a loop and **launch** the box: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-live-history.mp4" wait="2.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-live-history"} :::static println("live history launched") var phase = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 loop { visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { val y = sin(phase * 0.8) + 0.2 * sin(phase * 7.0) __m("live").history(y, dur = 120) } phase += 0.07 frame() } ``` The same loop is shorter written against the box's `time` instead of a phase it advances itself: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static loop { val t = time val y = sin(t * 0.8) + 0.2 * sin(t * 7.0) __m("live").history(y, dur = 120) frame() } ``` Run either as a launch, not a plain execute. ### Piano rolls in the editor The piano-roll visualizer is the same idea, but for scheduled notes rather than scalar values. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-pianoroll.mp4" wait="2.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-pianoroll"} :::static val arp = noteProcess { val chord = [48, 55, 60, 64] var step = 0 while (true) { note( pitch = chord[step % chord.size], duration = 0.18, velocity = 0.85, label = "n$step" ) rest(0.25) step++ } } println("inline piano roll launched") var playhead = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 loop { visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { __m("arp").pianoRoll(arp.at(playhead)) } playhead += 0.35 frame() } ``` Use it for sequencers, generative rhythm systems, or anything where you want to see future note structure without leaving the code. ## Display channels: the big canvas under the box Inline visuals sit beside one line of code. `display(...)` has the whole area under the box. Anything you pass to `display("channel", thing)` becomes HTML in a named output area. That HTML can be handwritten, auto-generated, interactive, or even an embedded browser/inspector. ### Raw HTML, pretty HTML, and heavy HTML - `display("channel", "
...
