Use `.h2` when you want to browse instead of read. That covers a large map, list, array or buffer without turning the output area into soup, and it covers your own data classes and Field's own types too. `.h2` on a plain object gives you its properties as a scrollable table: one row per property, with its declared type and its value. Above the table sit `outliner` and `columns` links, which open the same value in the full tree and column browsers. There is nothing to register; it reflects. If a property's getter throws, the row is still there, marked, with the exception text in its value cell. Four things are special-cased, because their fields are not where the interesting content is. A `Box` shows its name, frame, code size, run state, its whole property bag, and a table of its `parents`, `children`, `nested` and `nestedIn` edges. An `Fn` shows a sampled table of `x` and `f(x)` across its domain, because a function is its values and its one substantive field is a private closure. An `FLine` shows its node table: instruction kind, control-point count and endpoint per row. An exception shows its message, its cause chain and its stack. Some values `.h2` hands straight back to `.h`, because the compact rendering already *is* the value: numbers, strings, enums, a `Pair`, a vector, a matrix (which `.h` draws as a heatmap), and a `Quantity`, whose whole point is a number next to a unit. To see all of it at once, insert the **h2 Explorer Examples** template and run its boxes top to bottom. ### Markdown for captions and tables The escape hatch above has a way of taking over. A figure that wants a heading, a key/value table and a block of computed text ends up as a hundred lines of string concatenation, with a hand-picked font stack, a `` builder and a local `fun esc(s: String)`, often longer than the code it illustrates. `markdown("channel", "…")` says the same thing in markdown, and picks up Field's own `--field-*` tokens instead of re-inventing them: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-markdown.png" alt="one markdown card headed 'what the run settled on'. A two-column reading/value table gives tempo 122, drift -0.004 and voice 'saw 110 *'. Under it a status line reads stable, budget 83% used in amber, no retries. Then a two-column row labelled BEFORE and AFTER, holding gain 0.2 on the left and gain 0.9 on the right, and a quoted solver-output block reading 'converged in 41 steps, residual 3.2e-7'" wait="2.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="900" embed=true name="display-markdown"} :::static val readings = linkedMapOf("tempo" to 122, "drift" to -0.004, "voice" to "saw 110 *") val rows = readings.entries.joinToString("\n") { (k, v) -> "| ${k.md} | ${v.md} |" } val report = "converged in 41 steps\nresidual 3.2e-7" markdown("figure", """ ### what the run settled on | reading | value | |---------|-------| $rows status: {ok:**stable**} · budget: {warn:83% used} · {muted:no retries} :::row #### before ${mapOf("gain" to 0.2).h} --- #### after ${mapOf("gain" to 0.9).h} :::end #### solver output ~~~ $report ~~~ """, width = 820) println("markdown figure ready") ``` Three rules matter once a figure mixes computed values into the prose: - **HTML passes through, inline and block.** `.h`, `diffHtml()`, `graphSvg()` and friends already return HTML; interpolate them directly and they land verbatim, table cells included. Only text you actually wrote as markdown gets escaped. - **`value.md` for computed values.** Runtime values are not markdown — a `|` splits the row it lands in, a pair of `*` becomes emphasis, a `` is read as a tag and vanishes. Escape anything you did not write yourself. `mdEscape(value)` is the same function, written as a call. - **Fenced bodies are interpolated at column zero**, hard left, the way `$report` is above. Inside a fence whitespace is the content, and splicing at the surrounding indentation would indent only the value's first line. Beyond GitHub-flavoured markdown there are two additions: `:::row … :::end`, splitting columns on a `---` line, for the before/after shape markdown cannot spell; and `{role:text}` spans — `accent`, `muted`, `dim`, `ok`, `warn`, `bad` — so a callout never needs a hex literal. Neither applies inside code, so a `:::row` or a `{warn:…}` shown *as* an example stays as written. The figure above uses both: the before/after row, and the `ok`, `warn` and `muted` spans on its status line. You do not need `trimIndent()`; the text is dedented for you, and unlike `trimIndent` it survives having a multi-line value interpolated into it. `width` pins the card's width; without it the card is as wide as its widest unbreakable line. ### Trees and columns For a value you want to browse like a little filesystem, open it in a tree or column browser. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-display-browsers.png" alt="two inspector channels over the same nested scene map. 'columns' is a column browser, its root column listing camera, layers and palette with a scrollbar down the right of the pane" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1200" h="260" embed=true name="display-browsers"} :::static val scene = linkedMapOf( "camera" to linkedMapOf( "x" to 10, "y" to 20, "zoom" to 1.5, "active" to true ), "layers" to [ linkedMapOf( "name" to "dots", "visible" to true, "points" to [2, 4, 8, 16] ), linkedMapOf( "name" to "lines", "visible" to false, "style" to linkedMapOf("width" to 2, "color" to "#f2aa4c") ) ], "palette" to linkedMapOf( "background" to "#101820", "accent" to "#f2aa4c" ) ) tree("outline", scene) column("columns", scene) println("inspector panes ready") ``` - `tree("channel", value)` gives you an outline / tree browser. - `column("channel", value)` gives you a column-style browser. These are especially good for nested maps, scene graphs, structured JSON-like data, or anything you want to poke around in rather than summarize. Both take any value, not only maps and lists. A data class or one of your own classes opens to its public properties, an `IntArray` or `DoubleArray` opens to its elements, and a map whose keys are objects opens each entry to its key and its value. Every row shows its name, its type and a one-line summary (`5000 items`, `"label"`, `Point(x=1.0, y=2.5, label=p)`), so you can read most of a structure without opening anything: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-tree-values.png" alt="A tree embed titled LinkedHashMap, 4 entries, with a filter box. Open rows follow the value: if code that keeps running (a `frames { }` loop, say) adds to `particles`, the tree shows the new size within about a second, without re-running the box. An object that contains itself is marked with `↺` instead of being opened forever. Keys, once you have clicked into the embed: the arrow keys move and open (in `column`, `←` and `→` move between columns), `/` filters the rows, `c` copies the selected value as text, `p` copies the row's path, and `r` reloads. The header stays put while the rows scroll. The embed grows with its content up to a height and then scrolls; pass `maxHeight = 800` to `tree` or `column` to change that height. The rows are the same edges [`graphPaths`](graph_query.md) walks, so every row has a path from the value you passed in, such as `particle/position` or `many/250`. Press `p` (or the **path** button on a row) and paste it into box code: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val age = scene.graphPath("particle/age")?.get() ``` Type a pattern containing `/`, `*` or `|` into the filter and it runs `graphPaths` on the whole value instead of filtering one level: `**/tag` lists every `tag` at any depth, labelled by path. A row has no path when nothing reaches it by name: an element of a primitive array, a map key that is an object, the second of two map keys that print alike. A plain drag works like `vec2Control(...)`, and the callback gets each position. **Shift-drag** records a take: the whole stroke and its timing, kept with the box like any other control value. On a phone, tap **rec**, then draw. The trail of the take stays on the pad. The box replays the take, and the box keeps the time. `at(seconds)` returns where the take is that far into its loop, interpolated between the recorded samples, and `playhead(seconds)` puts a ring on the pad there. Read both off the clock in a `loop`, as the sequencer does, and the replay never drifts and keeps going with the browser closed. `initialTake` gives the pad something to play before you have recorded anything; here it is a figure eight: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-gesture.mp4" capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait-output="true" wait-output-kind="display" execution="launch" duration="4" fps="20" timeout="180" w="600" embed=true name="gesture" alt="an XY pad headed MOVE with the readout 2.0 s take and a rec button. Use `polar = true` when the value wraps around, like a phase or a hue. - Use `menu(...)` for choosing one of a few named options. - Use `gesture(...)` for a two-axis movement you want to perform once and loop. - For a curve over time you shape by hand, an envelope, use the keyframe editor, `keyframes(...)`: see [Keyframes and timelines](funFeatures.md#keyframes-and-timelines). It combines a waveform and native browser audio controls, keeps an optional vertical playhead synchronized with playback, and uses the waveform itself as a navigator: - click to seek; - drag to pan; - use the mouse wheel or `+` / `−` to zoom while keeping the visible playhead fixed on screen; - shift-wheel to pan; - double-click or press **all** to restore the complete clip. If the playhead is outside the visible interval, wheel zoom falls back to the pointer and button or keyboard zoom falls back to the center. Near the start or end of a recording, boundary clamping may move the playhead on screen. A completion-style spinner remains over the waveform while a newly zoomed or panned min/max envelope is loading, so the old waveform cannot be mistaken for the new view. During playback, crossing the right edge advances the visible interval and places the playhead slightly inside the new window; crossing the left edge after a backward seek mirrors that behavior. Set `followPlayhead = false` in `AudioVisualizerOptions` to keep a zoomed interval stationary. Waveform-envelope requests have a 15-second browser deadline; a stalled service clears the spinner and reports a timeout instead of leaving the view permanently busy. A strip underneath shows WebRTC voice activity, dBFS energy, and embedding novelty. Give the source `AudioVisualizer` and the speech view the same `syncGroup`. Audio playback moves a marker through both portraits; hovering either portrait publishes the nearest frame time; clicking seeks the player. The view also listens to `field-time-window`, so the waveform's visible interval stays saturated while the rest of the embedding path recedes. These are the same general `field-time-cursor`, `field-time-seek`, and `field-time-window` callbacks used by the timeline analysis views. ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} val sync = "field-recording-speech" display("source", audio.audioVisualizerHtml( options = AudioVisualizerOptions(syncGroup = sync), )) client.submit(wavlmBasePlusEmbeddingAnalysis(region, layer = 6)) .thenCompose(client::awaitAnalysis) .thenAccept { result -> display("WavLM", speechEmbeddingVisualizationHtml(result, syncGroup = sync)) } ``` Use `speechEmbeddingDashboardHtml(listOf(emotion2vec, wavlm), syncGroup = sync)` to compare both models on one playhead. `speechEmbeddingPreviewVisualizationHtml(...)` and `speechEmbeddingPreviewDashboardHtml(...)` are the no-fetch counterparts. The complete [speech-reactive embedding walkthrough](audio_ai_speech_embeddings.md) and `audio_ai_speech_embeddings` transcript show import → submit → monitor → await → audition. For a programmable local-neighbourhood projection, prefer `client.speechEmbeddingSmileTsnePreview(result, poolMillis = 500.0, hopMillis = 40.0)`. It downloads the result's binary MessagePack tensor, selects the requested time range before float16 expansion, mean-pools 500 ms of evidence around each point, and runs fixed-seed t-SNE inside Field using Smile. The independent 40 ms hop produces 25 points per second, just above a 24 fps display. Both values round to the model's native 20 ms grid; omit them to retain the original 50 Hz vectors. Pooling occurs before `maxFrames` sampling, and the visualizer header reports the effective pool, hop, distance, and projected frame count. The returned `AnalysisPreview` goes directly into the no-fetch visualizers. Exact classical MDS remains available through `speechEmbeddingSmilePreview`; both paths support cosine and Euclidean distance without rerunning the neural analysis. ### Short-time spectral phase portraits Three distance spaces from the [spectral walkthrough](audio_ai_spectral_embeddings.md): ![Three distance spaces](assets/audio_ai_spectral_embeddings/spectral_spaces.png) `spectralEmbeddingPreviewVisualizationHtml(preview)` uses the same two phase portraits and shared time bus for a Field-owned MDS or t-SNE projection of mel, log-mel, or MFCC frames. The lower strip shows energy, mel-distribution flux, and spectral centroid; path opacity follows normalized flux. Hovering reports time, energy, flux, centroid, and flatness, and clicking seeks any linked audio visualizer. One `analysis.embed_spectral` result contains all three representations, so decode once and create several views without another job: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} client.analysisPreview(result.id).thenCombineAsync( client.spectralEmbeddingFrames( result, durationSeconds = 10.0, poolMillis = 200.0, hopMillis = 40.0, ) ) { preview, frames -> [ SpectralEmbeddingDistance.MEL_WASSERSTEIN, SpectralEmbeddingDistance.LOG_MEL_COSINE, SpectralEmbeddingDistance.MFCC_EUCLIDEAN, ].map { distance -> preview.withSpectralProjection(frames.tsne(distance = distance, dimensions = 4)) } }.thenAccept { previews -> display("spaces", spectralEmbeddingPreviewDashboardHtml(previews, syncGroup = "recording")) } ``` The complete [short-time spectral walkthrough](audio_ai_spectral_embeddings.md) and `audio_ai_spectral_embeddings` transcript show source lookup/import → durable job → progress → binary artifact → temporal pooling → three Field Smile spaces → bidirectional audition. ### Instrument-labelled transcription A recording and its recovered notes from the [MuScriptor walkthrough](audio_ai_muscriptor.md): ![A recording and its recovered notes](assets/audio_ai_muscriptor/piano_roll.png) The same `analysisVisualizationHtml` viewer recognizes `analysis.transcribe_music` results as a MuScriptor piano roll. Note colour follows the recovered instrument group; the two lower lanes show active polyphony and onset count. It uses the same `syncGroup` time bus as the waveform, beat, pitch, speech-space, and spectral-space views, so playback, hover, seek, zoom, and pan stay aligned. ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} val sync = "recording-to-score" display("source", audio.audioVisualizerHtml( options = AudioVisualizerOptions(syncGroup = sync), )) display("score", analysisVisualizationHtml( transcription, syncGroup = sync, )) ``` The complete [MuScriptor walkthrough](audio_ai_muscriptor.md) and `audio_ai_muscriptor` transcript show the source lookup, typed request, durable job monitoring, synchronized result, typed MessagePack note access, and MIDI export. The same visualizer can begin with sound generated inside Field. `renderPatWav`, `renderDirtWav`, `renderDoughWav`, `renderFaustWavAsync`, and `recordSonicPiWav` all produce a `RenderedAudioFile`; `client.analyzeRenderedAudio(render)` imports it and returns a `RenderedAudioAnalysis` whose `visualizationHtml()` joins the playable waveform and every analysis lane on one sync group. The [render-to-analysis walkthrough](audio_render_analysis.md) and `audio_render_analysis` transcript show all five paths through submission and progress monitoring. ### Corpus neighbour microscope Retrieved neighbour windows from the [corpus walkthrough](audio_ai_corpus_microscope.md): ![Retrieved neighbour windows](assets/audio_ai_corpus_microscope/neighbours.png) `corpusMicroscopeHtml(preview, queryAudio)` composes the same general `AudioVisualizer` into a source-relative A/B board. Each neighbour retains its real asset and source timestamp, but every player uses `syncOffsetSeconds = -segment.startSeconds`; shared time zero is therefore the start of the selected window even when two windows come from different recordings. Hover, zoom, seek and playhead callbacks remain ordinary `field-time-*` events. The board adds no waveform transport of its own. It supplies exact ranges, grouped distance bars, and the immutable query-to-neighbour splice preview returned by Field Audio. That makes it useful as a general pattern for comparing aligned excerpts: produce a `CorpusPreview`, choose the query WAV representation, and let the range-aware player request only the visible envelopes. The [corpus microscope walkthrough](audio_ai_corpus_microscope.md) and `audio_ai_corpus_microscope` transcript show the complete index → submit → monitor → query → visualize path. ### Waveform-summary endpoint contract This player fetches its envelopes from the live Field Audio waveform endpoint. ![Service waveform envelopes of a Pat Dirt render](assets/audio_render_analysis/service_waveform.png) `AudioVisualizer` is not coupled to Field Audio. Any HTTP service can provide `waveformUrl`. The visualizer adds these query parameters whenever its visible interval changes: ```diffstatic {data-lang=text} start_seconds=12.5&duration_seconds=4.0&points=960 ``` The endpoint returns one min/max envelope per channel: ```diffstatic {data-lang=json} { "start_seconds": 12.5, "duration_seconds": 4.0, "sample_rate": 48000, "channels": 2, "point_count": 960, "minimum": [[-0.4, -0.2], [-0.3, -0.1]], "maximum": [[0.5, 0.3], [0.4, 0.2]] } ``` Each channel array must contain `point_count` values. The two-value arrays above are abbreviated. Keep the response cacheable: the component aborts stale requests while the user pans and asks for a fresh, pixel-sized envelope after zooming or resizing. ## Signal and synth visualizers Field's synth layer also comes with ready-made HTML and SVG visualizers for audio patches, scopes, envelopes, compressors, and related objects. These are display-based rather than inline, which is usually the right choice because they want a bit more space. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-signal-panels.png" alt="four synth panels in amber and blue on black. 'audio' pairs a dense stereo waveform at peak 0.858, rms 0.382 with a spectrum whose harmonics march up to a broad shelf past 5 kHz. 'scope' shows the same pair after filtering: a smaller waveform at peak 0.355 and a spectrum whose partials die away by 5 kHz. 'env' draws an ADSR, the orange gate dropping partway across and the blue level decaying after it, tagged RELEASE, lvl 0.401. 'comp' overlays an amber signal swelling into a compressor's blue gain-reduction curve, tagged GR 18.5 dB, threshold -18.0 dB, ratio 6.00:1" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="8" w="1200" h="350" trim=true embed=true name="signal-panels"} :::static import afield.audio.synth.* val sampleRate = 48_000f val frames = 512 val cycles = 16 val out = FloatArray(frames) fun renderSignal(signal: Signal) { repeat(cycles) { signal.render(out, frames, SynthContext(sampleRate, frames)) } } val audioScope = (saw / FreeVerb()).scope() renderSignal(audioScope) val monoScope = (saw / MoogLadder(cutoff = 900.p)).scope() renderSignal(monoScope) val g = Gate().also { it.open() } val env = ADSR(gate = g, release = 0.4.p) renderSignal(env) g.close() renderSignal(env) val comp = Compressor(threshold = (-18).p, ratio = 6.p) comp.input = saw * 0.35 renderSignal(comp) println("signal visualizers ready") display("audio", audioScope.summaryHtml(widthPx = 560, waveformHeightPx = 72, spectrumHeightPx = 72)) display("scope", monoScope.summaryHtml(widthPx = 560, waveformHeightPx = 72, spectrumHeightPx = 72)) display("env", env.stateSvg()) display("comp", comp.stateSvg()) ``` Good things to know here: - `patch.summaryHtml()` gives you a panel view of an audio patch. - `patch.liveSummary(...)` and `scope.liveSummary(...)` keep those panels moving while audio is running. - `scope.summaryHtml()` and `stereoScope.summaryHtml()` render wave/spectrum-style panels when you want a snapshot instead. - `env.stateSvg()` and `comp.stateSvg()` are compact SVG views for modulators / processors. - `noteProcess.pianoRollSvg()` is great when you want the piano roll in an output area instead of inline in the editor. So the choice is mostly about **where you want the visual to live**. ## Choosing between inline and display Here is the practical rule of thumb: - If the visual explains one line of code, put it inline on a stack mark (ᛟ, **Insert Stack Mark**). - If the visual explains a whole box or deserves interaction, put it in `display(...)`. - If the thing is large and structural, use `tree(...)`, `column(...)`, or `.h2`. - If the thing is tiny and human-readable, `.h` is often perfect. `histogram(...)` and `history(...)` return the value they were given, so you can leave them in a computation while you debug it. All of these tools compose. One box can have a little inline history, a piano roll, a browser in one output channel, and a control surface in another. Field is very happy when code is also an interface.

before:
name: autodiff_worked_example
description: >
  Loadable demo of Field's automatic-differentiation layer — afield.stdlib/autodiff.kt (reverse
  mode), autodiff_forward.kt (second-order forward mode), autodiff_optimize.kt (SGD / Adam /
  L-BFGS), autodiff_fn.kt (differentiating the Fn graph itself) and autodiff_geometry.kt (tracked
  vectors, planar IK, differentiable packing). Five pure-compute boxes, no Window and no Renderer:
  each draws into its own output channels via plot / showSignals / showPlaneGrid, all of which go
  through display() and so need neither AWT nor a GPU.
    1. autodiff_basics — grad { } on the Rosenbrock banana, then the same one-line expression
                    differentiated three ways that must agree: reverse mode (one tape sweep),
                    forward mode (a Dual2 Taylor number), and a central-difference oracle. The
                    second derivative comes free with the forward pass, so f, f' and f'' are all
                    plotted from one sweep. Also prints the exact 2x2 Hessian.
    2. autodiff_optimizers — the same Rosenbrock valley walked by SGD+momentum, Adam and L-BFGS,
                    with the three loss trajectories on one log-ish plot. L-BFGS reaches ~1e-30
                    in tens of iterations where the first-order methods are still crawling; the
                    point is not that L-BFGS is better but that a line search plus a curvature
                    model is a different *kind* of motion.
    3. autodiff_fn_fit — the Field-specific bridge. The SAME fitGradient() call, once with the
                    historic finite-difference gradient and once with gradient = EXACT, which
                    re-interprets the Fn graph in AD arithmetic. Same optimiser, same step size,
                    same landscape: the exact run reaches a lower RMSE for roughly a quarter of
                    the loss evaluations. Both curves are plotted against the target.
    4. autodiff_ik  — inverse kinematics on a four-link FLine chain: the rest pose, the solved
                    pose, and the solved-with-smoothness pose, in three panels sharing one window
                    so they are actually comparable. Forward kinematics is a cumulative angle sum,
                    which differentiates cleanly, so 18 L-BFGS iterations put the tip inside the
                    target ring. The third panel is the smoothness knob, which is an honest trade:
                    it straightens the pose and *costs* reach accuracy (0.006 units here).
    5. autodiff_pack — a differentiable circle packing: relu(overlap)^2 pairwise plus
                    relu(penetration)^2 against the walls. Before (a seeded scatter, worst overlap
                    48.3 units) and after (0.35 units) side by side. The residual is not solver
                    failure: the gentle pull toward the centre is a *competing* term, and 0.35 units
                    is where it balances the overlap hinge. Turn pullWeight to 0 and it goes away,
                    along with the compactness. This is also where the library's even-split kink
                    convention earns itself — at the instant two discs touch, the hinge's derivative
                    is half a one-sided rule's, so the packing settles instead of chattering across
                    the contact.
  Replay this file into a fresh Field with the agent backdoor (field_run_transcript) to see all
  five on screen, then move an IK target, turn the smoothness up, change a packing seed or swap
  L-BFGS for Adam and re-run a box. Each `execute` op omits inline code, so it runs the box's
  stored `code` property. Executed end-to-end by examples.demo-transcript.exec.
operations:
  - create:
      box: autodiff_basics
      name: reverse mode, forward mode, and the oracle
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 390.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // AD is not a new numeric tower you have to learn — it is ordinary Kotlin arithmetic on a
          // scalar that happens to remember how it was made. `grad { }` returns a *function*.
          val rosenbrock: (List<AD>) -> AD = { p -> (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq() }
          val gradient = grad(rosenbrock)
          val at = doubleArrayOf(-1.2, 1.0)

          // One expression, differentiated three ways that must agree.
          val xs = (0..300).map { it / 300.0 * 2.0 - 1.0 }
          val taylor = xs.map { x -> taylor2(x) { u -> exp(-u * u) * sin(6.0 * u) } }
          val reverse = xs.map { x -> derivative(x) { u -> exp(-u * u) * sin(6.0 * u) } }
          val oracle = xs.map { x ->
              val h = 1e-6
              val plain = { u: Double -> kotlin.math.exp(-u * u) * kotlin.math.sin(6.0 * u) }
              (plain(x + h) - plain(x - h)) / (2.0 * h)
          }
          val worstReverseVsForward = xs.indices.maxOf { kotlin.math.abs(taylor[it].first - reverse[it]) }
          val worstVsOracle = xs.indices.maxOf { kotlin.math.abs(reverse[it] - oracle[it]) }

          // f'' comes free with the forward pass, so all three curves are one sweep.
          showSignals(
              "f" to taylor.map { it.value },
              "f' (reverse mode)" to reverse,
              "f'' (forward mode)" to taylor.map { it.second },
              x = xs,
              channel = "1 derivatives",
              title = "exp(-x^2)*sin(6x), its slope and its curvature - one sweep, three orders",
              xTitle = "x"
          )

          // The exact Hessian, via forward-over-nothing: one Dual2 pass gives vT H v, and
          // polarisation recovers the off-diagonals. Not a finite difference of a gradient.
          val h = hessian(at) { p -> (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq() }

          "grad Rosenbrock at (-1.2, 1.0) = " + gradient(at).toList() + "\n" +
          "exact Hessian there = [[" + h[0][0] + ", " + h[0][1] + "], [" + h[1][0] + ", " + h[1][1] + "]]\n" +
          "reverse vs forward first derivative, worst of 301 samples: " + worstReverseVsForward + "\n" +
          "reverse vs central-difference oracle, worst of 301 samples: " + worstVsOracle

  - create:
      box: autodiff_optimizers
      name: three descents, one valley
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 1800.0, w: 300.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Rosenbrock's curved valley is the classic separator: a first-order method zig-zags
          // across it, a curvature model plus a line search walks along it.
          val rosenbrock: (List<AD>) -> AD = { p -> (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq() }
          val start = doubleArrayOf(-1.2, 1.0)
          val budget = 300

          val quiet = OptimizeOptions(iterations = budget, showProgress = false)
          val sgdRun = minimize(start, quiet.copy(method = OptimizeMethod.SGD, learningRate = 0.0012, momentum = 0.92), rosenbrock)
          val adamRun = minimize(start, quiet.copy(method = OptimizeMethod.ADAM, learningRate = 0.05), rosenbrock)
          val lbfgsRun = minimize(start, quiet.copy(method = OptimizeMethod.LBFGS), rosenbrock)

          // Losses span 30 orders of magnitude by the end, so plot log10 to see anything at all.
          fun logLoss(values: List<Double>) = values.map { kotlin.math.log10(kotlin.math.max(it, 1e-32)) }

          showSignals(
              "SGD + momentum" to logLoss(sgdRun.losses),
              "Adam" to logLoss(adamRun.losses),
              "L-BFGS" to logLoss(lbfgsRun.losses),
              channel = "1 trajectories",
              title = "log10 Rosenbrock loss per iteration, from (-1.2, 1.0)",
              xTitle = "iteration",
              yTitle = "log10 loss"
          )

          fun report(label: String, run: OptimizeRun) =
              label + ": value " + run.value + " at " + run.x.toList() +
              " after " + run.iterations + " iterations / " + run.evaluations +
              " evaluations (" + run.reason + ")"

          report("SGD+momentum", sgdRun) + "\n" +
          report("Adam", adamRun) + "\n" +
          report("L-BFGS", lbfgsRun)

  - create:
      box: autodiff_fn_fit
      name: exact gradients through the Fn graph
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 3600.0, w: 350.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.math.functions.Functions
          import afield.math.autodiff.FnGradientMode
          
          // Field's Fn is a closure over Double, so it cannot be differentiated by overloading its
          // arithmetic. But every Fn the stdlib builds carries an inspectable graph, and
          // autodiff_fn.kt re-interprets THAT in AD arithmetic. Before this existed, every gradient
          // in Field was a central difference.
          with(Functions) {
              val target = cos(2) * sin(1.5, amplitude = 0.8, offset = 0.2)
              val seed = cos(1.9) * sin(1.3, amplitude = 1.0)
          
              // Identical call, identical optimiser, identical step size. Only the gradient differs.
              val fd = fitGradient(target, seed, iterations = 400, lr = 0.05)
              val exact = fitGradient(target, seed, iterations = 400, lr = 0.05, gradient = FnGradientMode.EXACT)
          
              // The exact path never trusts itself: it re-checks its own interpreter against
              // Fn.eval on the loss grid before switching over, and refuses (or falls back under
              // AUTO) rather than returning a confident wrong gradient. Ask it why, for a seed
              // built from a piecewise oscillator it cannot differentiate:
              val refusal = exactFitRefusal(target, saw(1.0, amplitude = 0.8), Functions.Domain.DEFAULT)
          
              plot(target, channel = "1 target", title = "target   cos(2) * sin(1.5)")
              plot(exact.fitted, channel = "2 fitted", title = "fitted, exact reverse-mode gradients")
              showSignals(
                  "finite differences" to fd.losses,
                  "exact reverse mode" to exact.losses,
                  channel = "3 loss",
                  title = "RMSE per Adam step - same optimiser, different gradient",
                  xTitle = "step",
                  yTitle = "RMSE"
              )
          
              "finite differences: RMSE " + fd.initialError + " -> " + fd.finalError +
              " in " + fd.evaluations + " loss evaluations\n" +
              "exact reverse mode:  RMSE " + exact.initialError + " -> " + exact.finalError +
              " in " + exact.evaluations + " loss evaluations (usedExactGradient=" + exact.usedExactGradient + ")\n" +
              "a saw-based seed is refused, with a reason: " + refusal
          }
  - create:
      box: autodiff_ik
      name: inverse kinematics on an FLine chain
      frame: { x: 1400.0, y: 60.0, w: 350.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Forward kinematics is a cumulative sum of joint angles and a running position, which is
          // perfectly differentiable, so the inverse problem is just L-BFGS on |tip - target|^2.
          val chain = IkChain(vec(120.0, 300.0), doubleArrayOf(90.0, 80.0, 70.0, 55.0))
          val target = vec(330.0, 150.0)
          val restAngles = DoubleArray(chain.linkCount)

          val solved = solveIk(chain, target)
          val smoothed = solveIk(chain, target, options = IkOptions(smoothness = 2.0))

          // A ring *and* a cross, both wider than the chain's own joint dots, so "the tip landed on
          // the target" is visible rather than hidden under the end effector.
          fun marker(p: Vec2, r: Double) = fline {
              moveTo(p.x - r * 1.7, p.y); lineTo(p.x - r * 0.5, p.y)
              moveTo(p.x + r * 0.5, p.y); lineTo(p.x + r * 1.7, p.y)
              moveTo(p.x, p.y - r * 1.7); lineTo(p.x, p.y - r * 0.5)
              moveTo(p.x, p.y + r * 0.5); lineTo(p.x, p.y + r * 1.7)
              for (i in 0..40) {
                  val a = i / 40.0 * Math.PI * 2.0
                  val px = p.x + r * kotlin.math.cos(a)
                  val py = p.y + r * kotlin.math.sin(a)
                  if (i == 0) moveTo(px, py) else lineTo(px, py)
              }
              color = vec(1.0, 0.42, 0.3, 1.0)
              thickness = 2.0
          }
          fun pose(line: FLine, r: Double, g: Double, b: Double) = line.apply {
              color = vec(r, g, b, 1.0)
              thickness = 3.5
              pointed = true
              pointSize = 3.0
          }

          // One shared window, so the three panels are actually comparable.
          val window = Rect(40.0, 60.0, 400.0, 320.0)
          // 26 units across is wider than the chain's own joint dots at this window scale, so the
          // tip lands visibly *inside* the reticle rather than swallowing it.
          val cross = marker(target, 26.0)

          showPlaneGrid(
              "start pose\nall four joint angles zero - the arm points along +x" to
                  listOf(pose(chain.toFLine(restAngles), 0.45, 0.55, 0.72), cross),
              "solved\nreach error " + solved.reachError + " units, " + solved.run.iterations + " L-BFGS iterations" to
                  listOf(pose(chain.toFLine(solved.angles), 0.42, 0.86, 0.58), cross),
              "solved, smoothness = 2.0\nstraighter, and it costs " + smoothed.reachError + " units of reach" to
                  listOf(pose(chain.toFLine(smoothed.angles), 0.98, 0.86, 0.32), cross),
              channel = "1 poses",
              columns = 3,
              cellWidth = 260,
              window = window
          )
          showSignals(
              "reach loss" to solved.run.losses,
              channel = "2 loss",
              title = "|tip - target|^2 per L-BFGS iteration",
              xTitle = "iteration"
          )

          "solved joint angles (radians, relative link to link): " + solved.angles.toList() + "\n" +
          "tip landed at (" + solved.endEffector.x + ", " + solved.endEffector.y + "), target (" +
          target.x + ", " + target.y + "), error " + solved.reachError + "\n" +
          "with smoothness = 2.0 the pose straightens and the reach error rises to " + smoothed.reachError +
          " - the two terms genuinely compete, and reachError always tells the truth"

  - create:
      box: autodiff_pack
      name: a differentiable circle packing
      frame: { x: 1400.0, y: 1800.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Overlap is a hinge: relu(r1 + r2 - distance)^2, zero when the discs are disjoint and
          // growing quadratically once they interpenetrate. Walls are the same shape. Every term is
          // differentiable, so the packing is a descent rather than a relaxation loop of nudges.
          val radii = doubleArrayOf(38.0, 32.0, 30.0, 26.0, 24.0, 22.0, 20.0, 18.0, 16.0, 14.0, 12.0, 10.0)
          val boxWidth = 340.0
          val boxHeight = 250.0
          val packing = packCircles(radii, boxWidth, boxHeight, rngSeed = 5L)

          // run.initialX is the seeded scatter the descent started from, so "before" is real.
          val before = radii.indices.map {
              PackedCircle(vec(packing.run.initialX[2 * it], packing.run.initialX[2 * it + 1]), radii[it])
          }

          fun frame() = fline {
              moveTo(0.0, 0.0); lineTo(boxWidth, 0.0); lineTo(boxWidth, boxHeight); lineTo(0.0, boxHeight)
              close()
              color = vec(0.36, 0.44, 0.56, 0.7)
              thickness = 1.2
          }
          fun rings(circles: List<PackedCircle>, r: Double, g: Double, b: Double) = circles.map {
              it.toFLine(52).apply {
                  color = vec(r, g, b, 0.95)
                  thickness = 1.8
              }
          }

          fun worstOverlapOf(circles: List<PackedCircle>): Double {
              var worst = 0.0
              for (i in circles.indices) for (j in i + 1 until circles.size) {
                  val d = kotlin.math.hypot(
                      (circles[i].centre.x - circles[j].centre.x).toDouble(),
                      (circles[i].centre.y - circles[j].centre.y).toDouble()
                  )
                  worst = kotlin.math.max(worst, circles[i].radius + circles[j].radius - d)
              }
              return worst
          }

          val window = Rect(-20.0, -20.0, boxWidth + 40.0, boxHeight + 40.0)
          showPlaneGrid(
              "before\nseeded scatter, worst overlap " + worstOverlapOf(before) + " units" to
                  (rings(before, 0.52, 0.58, 0.72) + frame()),
              "after\n" + packing.run.iterations + " L-BFGS iterations, worst overlap " + packing.worstOverlap + " units" to
                  (rings(packing.circles, 0.42, 0.86, 0.62) + frame()),
              channel = "1 packing",
              columns = 2,
              cellWidth = 380,
              window = window
          )
          showSignals(
              "overlap + wall + pull loss" to packing.run.losses,
              channel = "2 loss",
              title = "packing loss per L-BFGS iteration",
              xTitle = "iteration"
          )

          "worst pairwise overlap " + worstOverlapOf(before) + " -> " + packing.worstOverlap + " units\n" +

after:
name: autodiff_worked_example
description: >
  Loadable demo of Field's automatic-differentiation layer — afield.stdlib/autodiff.kt (reverse
  mode), autodiff_forward.kt (second-order forward mode), autodiff_optimize.kt (SGD / Adam /
  L-BFGS), autodiff_fn.kt (differentiating the Fn graph itself) and autodiff_geometry.kt (tracked
  vectors, planar IK, differentiable packing). Five pure-compute boxes, no Window and no Renderer:
  each draws into its own output channels via plot / showSignals / showPlaneGrid, all of which go
  through display() and so need neither AWT nor a GPU.
    1. autodiff_basics — grad { } on the Rosenbrock banana, then the same one-line expression
                    differentiated three ways that must agree: reverse mode (one tape sweep),
                    forward mode (a Dual2 Taylor number), and a central-difference oracle. The
                    second derivative comes free with the forward pass, so f, f' and f'' are all
                    plotted from one sweep. Also prints the exact 2x2 Hessian.
    2. autodiff_optimizers — the same Rosenbrock valley walked by SGD+momentum, Adam and L-BFGS,
                    with the three loss trajectories on one log-ish plot. L-BFGS reaches ~1e-30
                    in tens of iterations where the first-order methods are still crawling; the
                    point is not that L-BFGS is better but that a line search plus a curvature
                    model is a different *kind* of motion.
    3. autodiff_fn_fit — the Field-specific bridge. The SAME fitGradient() call, once with the
                    historic finite-difference gradient and once with gradient = EXACT, which
                    re-interprets the Fn graph in AD arithmetic. Same optimiser, same step size,
                    same landscape: the exact run reaches a lower RMSE for roughly a quarter of
                    the loss evaluations. Both curves are plotted against the target.
    4. autodiff_ik  — inverse kinematics on a four-link FLine chain: the rest pose, the solved
                    pose, and the solved-with-smoothness pose, in three panels sharing one window
                    so they are actually comparable. Forward kinematics is a cumulative angle sum,
                    which differentiates cleanly, so 18 L-BFGS iterations put the tip inside the
                    target ring. The third panel is the smoothness knob, which is an honest trade:
                    it straightens the pose and *costs* reach accuracy (0.006 units here).
    5. autodiff_pack — a differentiable circle packing: relu(overlap)^2 pairwise plus
                    relu(penetration)^2 against the walls. Before (a seeded scatter, worst overlap
                    48.3 units) and after (0.35 units) side by side. The residual is not solver
                    failure: the gentle pull toward the centre is a *competing* term, and 0.35 units
                    is where it balances the overlap hinge. Turn pullWeight to 0 and it goes away,
                    along with the compactness. This is also where the library's even-split kink
                    convention earns itself — at the instant two discs touch, the hinge's derivative
                    is half a one-sided rule's, so the packing settles instead of chattering across
                    the contact.
  Replay this file into a fresh Field with the agent backdoor (field_run_transcript) to see all
  five on screen, then move an IK target, turn the smoothness up, change a packing seed or swap
  L-BFGS for Adam and re-run a box. Each `execute` op omits inline code, so it runs the box's
  stored `code` property. Executed end-to-end by examples.demo-transcript.exec.
operations:
  - create:
      box: autodiff_basics
      name: reverse mode, forward mode, and the oracle
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 390.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // AD is not a new numeric tower you have to learn — it is ordinary Kotlin arithmetic on a
          // scalar that happens to remember how it was made. `grad { }` returns a *function*.
          val rosenbrock: (List<AD>) -> AD = { p -> (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq() }
          val gradient = grad(rosenbrock)
          val at = doubleArrayOf(-1.2, 1.0)

          // One expression, differentiated three ways that must agree.
          val xs = (0..300).map { it / 300.0 * 2.0 - 1.0 }
          val taylor = xs.map { x -> taylor2(x) { u -> exp(-u * u) * sin(6.0 * u) } }
          val reverse = xs.map { x -> derivative(x) { u -> exp(-u * u) * sin(6.0 * u) } }
          val oracle = xs.map { x ->
              val h = 1e-6
              val plain = { u: Double -> kotlin.math.exp(-u * u) * kotlin.math.sin(6.0 * u) }
              (plain(x + h) - plain(x - h)) / (2.0 * h)
          }
          val worstReverseVsForward = xs.indices.maxOf { kotlin.math.abs(taylor[it].first - reverse[it]) }
          val worstVsOracle = xs.indices.maxOf { kotlin.math.abs(reverse[it] - oracle[it]) }

          // f'' comes free with the forward pass, so all three curves are one sweep.
          showSignals(
              "f" to taylor.map { it.value },
              "f' (reverse mode)" to reverse,
              "f'' (forward mode)" to taylor.map { it.second },
              x = xs,
              channel = "1 derivatives",
              title = "exp(-x^2)*sin(6x), its slope and its curvature - one sweep, three orders",
              xTitle = "x"
          )

          // The exact Hessian, via forward-over-nothing: one Dual2 pass gives vT H v, and
          // polarisation recovers the off-diagonals. Not a finite difference of a gradient.
          val h = hessian(at) { p -> (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq() }

          "grad Rosenbrock at (-1.2, 1.0) = " + gradient(at).toList() + "\n" +
          "exact Hessian there = [[" + h[0][0] + ", " + h[0][1] + "], [" + h[1][0] + ", " + h[1][1] + "]]\n" +
          "reverse vs forward first derivative, worst of 301 samples: " + worstReverseVsForward + "\n" +
          "reverse vs central-difference oracle, worst of 301 samples: " + worstVsOracle

  - create:
      box: autodiff_optimizers
      name: three descents, one valley
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 1800.0, w: 300.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Rosenbrock's curved valley is the classic separator: a first-order method zig-zags
          // across it, a curvature model plus a line search walks along it.
          val rosenbrock: (List<AD>) -> AD = { p -> (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq() }
          val start = doubleArrayOf(-1.2, 1.0)
          val budget = 300

          val quiet = OptimizeOptions(iterations = budget, showProgress = false)
          val sgdRun = minimize(start, quiet.copy(method = OptimizeMethod.SGD, learningRate = 0.0012, momentum = 0.92), rosenbrock)
          val adamRun = minimize(start, quiet.copy(method = OptimizeMethod.ADAM, learningRate = 0.05), rosenbrock)
          val lbfgsRun = minimize(start, quiet.copy(method = OptimizeMethod.LBFGS), rosenbrock)

          // Losses span 30 orders of magnitude by the end, so plot log10 to see anything at all.
          fun logLoss(values: List<Double>) = values.map { kotlin.math.log10(kotlin.math.max(it, 1e-32)) }

          showSignals(
              "SGD + momentum" to logLoss(sgdRun.losses),
              "Adam" to logLoss(adamRun.losses),
              "L-BFGS" to logLoss(lbfgsRun.losses),
              channel = "1 trajectories",
              title = "log10 Rosenbrock loss per iteration, from (-1.2, 1.0)",
              xTitle = "iteration",
              yTitle = "log10 loss"
          )

          fun report(label: String, run: OptimizeRun) =
              label + ": value " + run.value + " at " + run.x.toList() +
              " after " + run.iterations + " iterations / " + run.evaluations +
              " evaluations (" + run.reason + ")"

          report("SGD+momentum", sgdRun) + "\n" +
          report("Adam", adamRun) + "\n" +
          report("L-BFGS", lbfgsRun)

  - create:
      box: autodiff_fn_fit
      name: exact gradients through the Fn graph
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 3600.0, w: 350.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.math.functions.Functions
          import afield.math.autodiff.FnGradientMode
          
          // Field's Fn is a closure over Double, so it cannot be differentiated by overloading its
          // arithmetic. But every Fn the stdlib builds carries an inspectable graph, and
          // autodiff_fn.kt re-interprets THAT in AD arithmetic. Before this existed, every gradient
          // in Field was a central difference.
          with(Functions) {
              val target = cos(2) * sin(1.5, amplitude = 0.8, offset = 0.2)
              val seed = cos(1.9) * sin(1.3, amplitude = 1.0)
          
              // Identical call, identical optimiser, identical step size. Only the gradient differs.
              val fd = fitGradient(target, seed, iterations = 400, lr = 0.05)
              val exact = fitGradient(target, seed, iterations = 400, lr = 0.05, gradient = FnGradientMode.EXACT)
          
              // The exact path never trusts itself: it re-checks its own interpreter against
              // Fn.eval on the loss grid before switching over, and refuses (or falls back under
              // AUTO) rather than returning a confident wrong gradient. Ask it why, for a seed
              // built from a piecewise oscillator it cannot differentiate:
              val refusal = exactFitRefusal(target, saw(1.0, amplitude = 0.8), Functions.Domain.DEFAULT)
          
              plot(target, channel = "1 target", title = "target   cos(2) * sin(1.5)")
              plot(exact.fitted, channel = "2 fitted", title = "fitted, exact reverse-mode gradients")
              showSignals(
                  "finite differences" to fd.losses,
                  "exact reverse mode" to exact.losses,
                  channel = "3 loss",
                  title = "RMSE per Adam step - same optimiser, different gradient",
                  xTitle = "step",
                  yTitle = "RMSE"
              )
          
              "finite differences: RMSE " + fd.initialError + " -> " + fd.finalError +
              " in " + fd.evaluations + " loss evaluations\n" +
              "exact reverse mode:  RMSE " + exact.initialError + " -> " + exact.finalError +
              " in " + exact.evaluations + " loss evaluations (usedExactGradient=" + exact.usedExactGradient + ")\n" +
              "a saw-based seed is refused, with a reason: " + refusal
          }
  - create:
      box: autodiff_ik
      name: inverse kinematics on an FLine chain
      frame: { x: 1400.0, y: 60.0, w: 350.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Forward kinematics is a cumulative sum of joint angles and a running position, which is
          // perfectly differentiable, so the inverse problem is just L-BFGS on |tip - target|^2.
          val chain = IkChain(vec(120.0, 300.0), doubleArrayOf(90.0, 80.0, 70.0, 55.0))
          val target = vec(330.0, 150.0)
          val restAngles = DoubleArray(chain.linkCount)

          val solved = solveIk(chain, target)
          val smoothed = solveIk(chain, target, options = IkOptions(smoothness = 2.0))

          // A ring *and* a cross, both wider than the chain's own joint dots, so "the tip landed on
          // the target" is visible rather than hidden under the end effector.
          fun marker(p: Vec2, r: Double) = fline {
              moveTo(p.x - r * 1.7, p.y); lineTo(p.x - r * 0.5, p.y)
              moveTo(p.x + r * 0.5, p.y); lineTo(p.x + r * 1.7, p.y)
              moveTo(p.x, p.y - r * 1.7); lineTo(p.x, p.y - r * 0.5)
              moveTo(p.x, p.y + r * 0.5); lineTo(p.x, p.y + r * 1.7)
              circle(p.x, p.y, r, segments = 40)
              color = vec(1.0, 0.42, 0.3, 1.0)
              thickness = 2.0
          }
          fun pose(line: FLine, r: Double, g: Double, b: Double) = line.apply {
              color = vec(r, g, b, 1.0)
              thickness = 3.5
              pointed = true
              pointSize = 3.0
          }

          // One shared window, so the three panels are actually comparable.
          val window = Rect(40.0, 60.0, 400.0, 320.0)
          // 26 units across is wider than the chain's own joint dots at this window scale, so the
          // tip lands visibly *inside* the reticle rather than swallowing it.
          val cross = marker(target, 26.0)

          showPlaneGrid(
              "start pose\nall four joint angles zero - the arm points along +x" to
                  listOf(pose(chain.toFLine(restAngles), 0.45, 0.55, 0.72), cross),
              "solved\nreach error " + solved.reachError + " units, " + solved.run.iterations + " L-BFGS iterations" to
                  listOf(pose(chain.toFLine(solved.angles), 0.42, 0.86, 0.58), cross),
              "solved, smoothness = 2.0\nstraighter, and it costs " + smoothed.reachError + " units of reach" to
                  listOf(pose(chain.toFLine(smoothed.angles), 0.98, 0.86, 0.32), cross),
              channel = "1 poses",
              columns = 3,
              cellWidth = 260,
              window = window
          )
          showSignals(
              "reach loss" to solved.run.losses,
              channel = "2 loss",
              title = "|tip - target|^2 per L-BFGS iteration",
              xTitle = "iteration"
          )

          "solved joint angles (radians, relative link to link): " + solved.angles.toList() + "\n" +
          "tip landed at (" + solved.endEffector.x + ", " + solved.endEffector.y + "), target (" +
          target.x + ", " + target.y + "), error " + solved.reachError + "\n" +
          "with smoothness = 2.0 the pose straightens and the reach error rises to " + smoothed.reachError +
          " - the two terms genuinely compete, and reachError always tells the truth"

  - create:
      box: autodiff_pack
      name: a differentiable circle packing
      frame: { x: 1400.0, y: 1800.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Overlap is a hinge: relu(r1 + r2 - distance)^2, zero when the discs are disjoint and
          // growing quadratically once they interpenetrate. Walls are the same shape. Every term is
          // differentiable, so the packing is a descent rather than a relaxation loop of nudges.
          val radii = doubleArrayOf(38.0, 32.0, 30.0, 26.0, 24.0, 22.0, 20.0, 18.0, 16.0, 14.0, 12.0, 10.0)
          val boxWidth = 340.0
          val boxHeight = 250.0
          val packing = packCircles(radii, boxWidth, boxHeight, rngSeed = 5L)

          // run.initialX is the seeded scatter the descent started from, so "before" is real.
          val before = radii.indices.map {
              PackedCircle(vec(packing.run.initialX[2 * it], packing.run.initialX[2 * it + 1]), radii[it])
          }

          fun frame() = fline {
              rect(0.0, 0.0, boxWidth, boxHeight)
              color = vec(0.36, 0.44, 0.56, 0.7)
              thickness = 1.2
          }
          fun rings(circles: List<PackedCircle>, r: Double, g: Double, b: Double) = circles.map {
              it.toFLine(52).apply {
                  color = vec(r, g, b, 0.95)
                  thickness = 1.8
              }
          }

          fun worstOverlapOf(circles: List<PackedCircle>): Double {
              var worst = 0.0
              for (i in circles.indices) for (j in i + 1 until circles.size) {
                  val d = kotlin.math.hypot(
                      (circles[i].centre.x - circles[j].centre.x).toDouble(),
                      (circles[i].centre.y - circles[j].centre.y).toDouble()
                  )
                  worst = kotlin.math.max(worst, circles[i].radius + circles[j].radius - d)
              }
              return worst
          }

          val window = Rect(-20.0, -20.0, boxWidth + 40.0, boxHeight + 40.0)
          showPlaneGrid(
              "before\nseeded scatter, worst overlap " + worstOverlapOf(before) + " units" to
                  (rings(before, 0.52, 0.58, 0.72) + frame()),
              "after\n" + packing.run.iterations + " L-BFGS iterations, worst overlap " + packing.worstOverlap + " units" to
                  (rings(packing.circles, 0.42, 0.86, 0.62) + frame()),
              channel = "1 packing",
              columns = 2,
              cellWidth = 380,
              window = window
          )
          showSignals(
              "overlap + wall + pull loss" to packing.run.losses,
              channel = "2 loss",
              title = "packing loss per L-BFGS iteration",
              xTitle = "iteration"
          )

          "worst pairwise overlap " + worstOverlapOf(before) + " -> " + packing.worstOverlap + " units\n" +
          "worst escape beyond the box wall: " + packing.worstEscape + " units\n" +
          "loss " + packing.run.initialValue + " -> " + packing.run.value +
          " in " + packing.run.iterations + " iterations (" + packing.run.reason + ")"

before:
name: fline_measure
description: >
  Measuring, trimming and crossing an FLine, the companion to the "Measuring along a line",
  "Trimming and splitting by distance" and "Crossings, bounds and orientation" sections of
  `public/docs/fline_examples.md`. Five boxes: evenly spaced locations with normals and
  osculating circles; trim and splitAt; crossings, selfCrossings and tight bounds; and
  contains2D under the non-zero and even-odd fill rules; and the 3D frame (tangent, normal,
  binormal, curvature) along a helix. Run each box; each draws into `lines`.
operations:
  - create:
      box: fline-measure-locate
      name: 1 - Locations along a line
      frame:
        x: 60.0
        y: 60.0
        w: 420.0
        h: 100.0
      properties:
        code: |
          val curve = fline {
              moveTo(40, 210)
              cubicTo(90, 30, 230, 30, 260, 140)
              cubicTo(280, 220, 360, 230, 390, 90)
              thickness = 2.0
              color = vec(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0)
          }

          // thirteen locations, evenly spaced by distance
          val stops = (0..12).mapNotNull { curve.locationAtFraction(it / 12f) }

          val normals = stops.map { loc ->
              fline {
                  moveTo(loc.point.x, loc.point.y)
                  lineTo(loc.point.x + loc.normal2D.x * 22, loc.point.y + loc.normal2D.y * 22)
                  thickness = 1.5
                  color = vec(0.4, 0.9, 1.0, 1.0)
              }
          }

          // the circle that matches the bend, at three of them
          val bends = listOf(stops[3], stops[7], stops[10]).map { loc ->
              val r = 1.0 / loc.signedCurvature2D
              fline {
                  circle(loc.point.x + loc.normal2D.x * r, loc.point.y + loc.normal2D.y * r, kotlin.math.abs(r))
                  thickness = 1.0
                  color = vec(1.0, 0.6, 0.2, 0.8)
              }
          }

          lines(listOf(curve) + normals + bends, w = 420.0, h = 260.0, fitToSize = true)
  - create:
      box: fline-measure-trim
      name: 2 - Trim and split by distance
      frame:
        x: 520.0
        y: 60.0
        w: 420.0
        h: 100.0
      properties:
        code: |
          val curve = fline {
              moveTo(40, 200)
              cubicTo(100, 20, 220, 20, 250, 130)
              lineTo(380, 60)
              thickness = 1.0
              color = vec(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.35)
          }

          val total = curve.length()

          // from a quarter to 60% of the way, by distance, drawn over the original
          val middle = curve.trim(0.25f * total, 0.6f * total).apply {
              thickness = 5.0
              color = vec(0.4, 0.9, 1.0, 1.0)
          }

          // cut at 100 units: two pieces whose lengths add up to the whole
          val (head, tail) = curve.splitAt(100f)
          head.apply { thickness = 2.0; color = vec(1.0, 0.6, 0.2, 1.0) }

          print("total ${"%.1f".format(total)} = ${"%.1f".format(head.length())} + ${"%.1f".format(tail.length())}")

          lines(listOf(curve, head, middle), w = 420.0, h = 260.0, fitToSize = true)
  - create:
      box: fline-measure-cross
      name: 3 - Crossings, bounds, orientation
      frame:
        x: 60.0
        y: 520.0
        w: 420.0
        h: 100.0
      properties:
        code: |
          val loop = fline {
              moveTo(60, 200)
              cubicTo(420, 40, 0, 40, 340, 210)
              thickness = 2.0
              color = vec(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0)
          }

          val ring = fline {
              circle(200, 130, 70)
              thickness = 2.0
              color = vec(0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.0)
          }

          // where the loop crosses the ring, and where it crosses itself
          val hits = listOf(loop.crossings2D(ring), loop.selfCrossings2D()).flatten().map { it.point }
          val dots = polylineFrom(hits.map { it.v2 }).apply {
              pointed = true
              pointSize = 3.0
              stroked = false
              color = vec(1.0, 0.5, 0.2, 1.0)
          }

          // bounds that hug the curve, against the control-point bounds
          val tight = fline { rect(loop.tightBounds2D()); thickness = 1.0; color = vec(0.4, 1.0, 0.6, 1.0) }
          val loose = fline { rect(loop.fast2DBounds()); thickness = 1.0; color = vec(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.25) }

          print("${hits.size} crossings; clockwise on screen: ${ring.isClockwise2D()}")

          lines(listOf(loose, tight, ring, loop, dots), w = 420.0, h = 260.0, fitToSize = true)
  - create:
      box: fline-measure-fill
      name: 4 - Fill rules that follow the curve
      frame:
        x: 520.0
        y: 520.0
        w: 420.0
        h: 100.0
      properties:
        code: |
          // two circles drawn the same way round: a ring
          fun ring(dx: Double) = fline {
              circle(110 + dx, 120, 95)
              circle(110 + dx, 120, 40)
              thickness = 2.0
              color = vec(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0)
          }

          // dots that are inside under each fill rule: non-zero on the left, even-odd on the right
          fun insideDots(dx: Double, rule: FLineFillRule) = fline {
              val shape = ring(dx)
              for (i in 0..24) for (j in 0..24) {
                  val p = Vec2((15 + dx + i * 8).toFloat(), (25 + j * 8).toFloat())
                  if (shape.contains2D(p, rule)) { moveTo(p.x, p.y); lineTo(p.x + 0.01, p.y) }
              }
              pointed = true
              pointSize = 0.7
              stroked = false
              color = vec(1.0, 0.6, 0.2, 1.0)
          }

          lines(listOf(ring(0.0), ring(240.0), insideDots(0.0, FLineFillRule.NonZero), insideDots(240.0, FLineFillRule.EvenOdd)),
              w = 460.0, h = 240.0, fitToSize = true)
  - create:
      box: fline-measure-helix
      name: 5 - A 3D frame along a helix
      frame:
        x: 60.0
        y: 980.0
        w: 420.0
        h: 100.0
      properties:
        code: |
          // a helix of radius 80 rising 30 units per turn, one cubic per quarter turn
          val r = 80.0
          val rise = 30.0
          val k = 0.5522847 * r
          val helix = fline {
              moveTo(r, 0, 0)
              for (q in 0 until 12) {
                  val a0 = q * PI / 2
                  val a1 = a0 + PI / 2
                  val z0 = rise * q / 4
                  val z1 = rise * (q + 1) / 4
                  cubicTo(
                      r * cos(a0) - k * sin(a0), r * sin(a0) + k * cos(a0), z0 + (z1 - z0) / 3,
                      r * cos(a1) + k * sin(a1), r * sin(a1) - k * cos(a1), z0 + 2 * (z1 - z0) / 3,
                      r * cos(a1), r * sin(a1), z1,
                  )
              }
          }

          // look at it from the side and a little above: x across, z up, y into the page
          fun view(p: Vec3) = vec(p.x + 0.35 * p.y, -p.z - 0.35 * p.y)

          val drawn = fline {
              helix.sampleByNumber(400).forEachIndexed { i, p -> if (i == 0) moveTo(view(p)) else lineTo(view(p)) }
              thickness = 1.5
              color = vec(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0)

# Boolean networks to FLine examples

*Every public declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference: [`booleannetworks.kt`](reference/data.md#booleannetworks-kt). Start from [what's already in the box](reference/index.md).*

A Boolean network is a set of nodes that are each on or off, plus a rule that computes every node's next value from the current values of the others. Because there are only finitely many states, every run ends up in a loop or at a fixed point (an *attractor*), and Field can list them all exactly. Each example below draws the network's wiring next to what it does over time.

## Wiring and state-space, side by side

`toggleNetwork()` is two nodes, `A = NOT B` and `B = A`, and that is already enough to separate the two views the rest of the page relies on: the causal wiring graph, which has one arrow per dependency, and the induced state-transition graph, which has one arrow per state.

## Boolean attractors as drum grids

A limit cycle repeats on a fixed period, so it is already a rhythm. You can treat each node as a lane directly, or gate the cycle with a beat phase such as `step % 4` and turn the same binary motion into kick / snare / hat style triggers.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/boolean_networks_examples/rhythm_cycles.png" wait="1.0" capture="box"}
import afield.geometry.path.FLine

data class RhythmCandidate(val seed: Int, val net: BooleanNetwork, val attr: Attractor, val score: Double)

fun activity(attr: Attractor, net: BooleanNetwork): Double =
    attr.cycle.sumOf { state -> state.count { it } }.toDouble() / (attr.period * net.size).toDouble()

val candidate =

        val net = kauffmanNetwork(n = 5, k = 2, seed = seed.toLong())
        net.findAttractors()
            .filter { it.period in 5..10 }
            .map { attr ->
                val density = activity(attr, net)
                val periodScore = 1.0 - kotlin.math.abs(attr.period - 8) / 8.0
                val densityScore = 1.0 - kotlin.math.abs(density - 0.42)
                val basinScore = attr.basin.size.toDouble() / (1 shl net.size).toDouble()
                RhythmCandidate(seed, net, attr, periodScore * 1.6 + densityScore * 1.2 + basinScore)
            }
            .maxByOrNull { it.score }
    }.maxByOrNull { it.score }!!

val natural = candidate.attr.repeatedCycle(16)

            state[2] && step % 2 == 0,
            state[3] && (step % 8 == 4 || step % 8 == 12),

    lineTo(x, y + h)
    close()
```

# Boolean networks to FLine examples

*Every public declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference: [`booleannetworks.kt`](reference/data.md#booleannetworks-kt). Start from [what's already in the box](reference/index.md).*

A Boolean network is a set of nodes that are each on or off, plus a rule that computes every node's next value from the current values of the others. Because there are only finitely many states, every run ends up in a loop or at a fixed point (an *attractor*), and Field can list them all exactly. Each example below draws the network's wiring next to what it does over time.

## Wiring and state-space, side by side

`toggleNetwork()` is two nodes, `A = NOT B` and `B = A`, and that is already enough to separate the two views the rest of the page relies on: the causal wiring graph, which has one arrow per dependency, and the induced state-transition graph, which has one arrow per state.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/boolean_networks_examples/toggle_state_space.png" wait="1.0" capture="box"}
:::static
import afield.geometry.path.FLine

val net = toggleNetwork()
val attrs = net.findAttractors()

:::fold helpers: offset a drawing, fill a background panel
fun shift(lines: List<FLine>, dx: Double, dy: Double) = lines.map { it + vec(dx, dy, 0) }

fun panel(x: Double, y: Double, w: Double, h: Double, color: Vec4) = fline {
    rect(x, y, w, h)
    filled = true
    stroked = true
    thickness = 1.0
    this.color = color
}
:::endfold

lines(
    [
        panel(30.0, 40.0, 430.0, 430.0, vec(0.08, 0.13, 0.18, 0.56)),
        panel(500.0, 40.0, 500.0, 430.0, vec(0.16, 0.11, 0.08, 0.54)),
    ] +
        shift(net.drawNetworkGraph(radius = 120.0, nodeR = 18.0), 80.0, 80.0) +
        shift(net.drawStateTransitionGraph(radius = 150.0), 560.0, 55.0),
    channel = "boolean-toggle",
    w = 1060.0,
    h = 520.0,
    fitToSize = true
)
```

The left image tells you what depends on what; the right image tells you what that dependency does to every possible state. Here the two coincide: with four states and both nodes reading the other, the whole state space is a single period-4 loop, `00 -> 10 -> 11 -> 01` and back.

## Segment-polarity basins and a transient

`segmentPolarityNetwork()` has four nodes, so sixteen states, and unlike the toggle it does not spend all of them on one cycle. There is more than one attractor, so there is more than one *basin*: the set of starting states that end on a given attractor.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/boolean_networks_examples/segment_basins.png" wait="1.0" capture="box"}

val cycleStates = largest.cycle.map { net.stateToInt(it) }.toSet()
val start = largest.basin.firstOrNull { it !in cycleStates } ?: largest.basin.first()
val trajectory = net.trajectoryUntilCycle(net.intToState(start))
val shown = attrs.take(2)
```

The left panel is one concrete transient, the middle panel is the whole 16-state transition graph, and the right panel samples the two largest basins as miniature spacetime strips. ## Random Kauffman regimes as a plotted sweep

The two networks above were hand-made. This one asks a population question instead: as in-degree `k` rises in random `N-K` Kauffman systems, what happens to the typical attractor count and period?

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/boolean_networks_examples/kauffman_sweep.png" wait="1.0" capture="box"}
:::static
import afield.geometry.path.FLine

data class SweepRow(val k: Int, val attractors: Double, val period: Double, val fixed: Double)

val rows = (1..5).map { k ->
    val runs = (0 until 18).map { seed ->
        val attrs = kauffmanNetwork(n = 8, k = k, seed = seed.toLong()).findAttractors()
        Triple(
            attrs.size.toDouble(),
            if (attrs.isEmpty()) 0.0 else attrs.map { it.period.toDouble() }.average(),
            attrs.count { it.period == 1 }.toDouble(),
        )
    }
    SweepRow(
        k = k,
        attractors = runs.map { it.first }.average(),
        period = runs.map { it.second }.average(),
        fixed = runs.map { it.third }.average(),
    )
}

:::fold plot helpers: shared y scale, axes and grid, polylines, square markers
val maxY = [
    rows.maxOf { it.attractors },
    rows.maxOf { it.period },
    rows.maxOf { it.fixed }
].max() + 0.5

fun guides() = [
    fline {
        moveTo(80, 580); lineTo(1100, 580)
        moveTo(80, 120); lineTo(80, 580)
        color = vec(1, 1, 1, 0.22)
        thickness = 1.1
    },
    fline {
        for (i in 0..8) {
            val y = 580.0 - i / 8.0 * 430.0
            moveTo(80, y); lineTo(1100, y)
        }
        for (i in rows.indices) {
            val x = 80.0 + i.toDouble() / (rows.size - 1).coerceAtLeast(1).toDouble() * 1020.0
            moveTo(x, 120.0); lineTo(x, 580.0)
        }
        color = vec(1, 1, 1, 0.08)
        thickness = 1.0
    }
]

fun curve(values: List<Double>, color: Vec4, thickness: Double): FLine = fline {
    breakNext()
    values.forEachIndexed { i, value ->
        val x = 80.0 + i.toDouble() / (values.size - 1).coerceAtLeast(1).toDouble() * 1020.0
        val y = 580.0 - value / maxY * 430.0
        lineTo(x, y)
    }
    this.color = color
    this.thickness = thickness
}

fun markers(values: List<Double>, color: Vec4, size: Double): FLine = fline {
    filled = true
    stroked = false
    values.forEachIndexed { i, value ->
        val x = 80.0 + i.toDouble() / (values.size - 1).coerceAtLeast(1).toDouble() * 1020.0
        val y = 580.0 - value / maxY * 430.0
        rect(x - size, y - size, 2 * size, 2 * size)
    }
    this.color = color
}
:::endfold

lines(
    guides() + [
        curve(rows.map { it.attractors }, vec(0.56, 0.92, 1.0, 0.95), 3.0),
        curve(rows.map { it.period }, vec(1.0, 0.74, 0.38, 0.92), 3.0),
        curve(rows.map { it.fixed }, vec(0.58, 1.0, 0.68, 0.92), 3.0),
        markers(rows.map { it.attractors }, vec(0.56, 0.92, 1.0, 0.95), 5.0),
        markers(rows.map { it.period }, vec(1.0, 0.74, 0.38, 0.92), 5.0),
        markers(rows.map { it.fixed }, vec(0.58, 1.0, 0.68, 0.92), 5.0),
    ],
    channel = "boolean-kauffman",
    w = 1180.0,
    h = 660.0,
    fitToSize = true
)
```

The plot has no legend, so: blue is the mean number of attractors, orange the mean period, green the mean number of fixed points, each averaged over 18 seeds at `n = 8` for `k` from 1 to 5, and all three share one y scale. All three rise with `k`: more connections give more attractors and longer ones. Orange overtakes blue around the middle of the sweep and turns down at `k = 5`, and green stays under blue throughout, as it has to: a fixed point is a period-1 attractor and so is counted in both.

## Boolean attractors as drum grids

A limit cycle repeats on a fixed period, so it is already a rhythm. You can treat each node as a lane directly, or gate the cycle with a beat phase such as `step % 4` and turn the same binary motion into kick / snare / hat style triggers.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/boolean_networks_examples/rhythm_cycles.png" wait="1.0" capture="box"}
:::static
import afield.geometry.path.FLine

data class RhythmCandidate(val seed: Int, val net: BooleanNetwork, val attr: Attractor, val score: Double)

fun activity(attr: Attractor, net: BooleanNetwork): Double =
    attr.cycle.sumOf { state -> state.count { it } }.toDouble() / (attr.period * net.size).toDouble()

val candidate =
    (0..240).mapNotNull { seed ->
        val net = kauffmanNetwork(n = 5, k = 2, seed = seed.toLong())
        net.findAttractors()
            .filter { it.period in 5..10 }
            .map { attr ->
                val density = activity(attr, net)
                val periodScore = 1.0 - kotlin.math.abs(attr.period - 8) / 8.0
                val densityScore = 1.0 - kotlin.math.abs(density - 0.42)
                val basinScore = attr.basin.size.toDouble() / (1 shl net.size).toDouble()
                RhythmCandidate(seed, net, attr, periodScore * 1.6 + densityScore * 1.2 + basinScore)
            }
            .maxByOrNull { it.score }
    }.maxByOrNull { it.score }!!

val natural = candidate.attr.repeatedCycle(16)
val gated =
    natural.mapIndexed { step, state ->
        booleanArrayOf(
            state[0] && step % 4 == 0,
            state[1] && step % 4 == 2,
            state[2] && step % 2 == 0,
            state[3] && (step % 8 == 4 || step % 8 == 12),
            state[4] && (step % 4 == 1 || step % 4 == 3),
        )
    }

:::fold helpers: offset a drawing, fill a background panel
fun shift(lines: List<FLine>, dx: Double, dy: Double) = lines.map { it + vec(dx, dy, 0) }

fun panel(x: Double, y: Double, w: Double, h: Double, color: Vec4) = fline {
    rect(x, y, w, h)
    filled = true
    stroked = true
    thickness = 1.0
    this.color = color
}
:::endfold

lines(
    [
        panel(30.0, 40.0, 280.0, 420.0, vec(0.08, 0.13, 0.18, 0.56)),
        panel(350.0, 40.0, 470.0, 420.0, vec(0.10, 0.10, 0.14, 0.56)),
        panel(860.0, 40.0, 470.0, 420.0, vec(0.16, 0.11, 0.08, 0.54)),
    ] +
        shift(candidate.net.drawNetworkGraph(radius = 96.0, nodeR = 17.0), 76.0, 118.0) +
        shift(drawRhythmGrid(natural, cellW = 21.0, cellH = 22.0, stepGap = 5.0, laneGap = 9.0, accentEvery = 4), 390.0, 150.0) +

    channel = "boolean-rhythm",
    w = 1380.0,
    h = 520.0,
    fitToSize = true
)
```

The middle grid is the raw attractor repeated over two bars. The right grid is the same cycle clock-gated into five kick / snare / hat / clap / percussion lanes, ready to hand to a sampler.
